### 1. Which provinces and territories signed bilateral agreements, when, for how much, and what happened to the rest

_(to write)_ About 1500 words.

### 2. What the agreements actually cover — drug lists, devices, cost-sharing — and what the Act's other obligations (expert committee, essential drugs list, bulk purchasing, appropriate-use strategy) have produced

_(to write)_ About 1300 words.

### 3. How many people are actually covered and using it: implementation dates, enrolment and claims figures, and what is not counted

_(to write)_ About 1300 words.

### 4. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer says the full single-payer program would cost, and how the first-phase estimate differs

Two PBO numbers get quoted constantly in this debate and they answer different questions. Keeping them apart is most of the analytical work.

**The full single-payer plan.** The PBO's *Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan* (report RP-2324-016-S, released 12 October 2023) is the reference costing for a complete program. It is not a costing of the Pharmacare Act; it predates the Act by a year, and it was written in response to parliamentary interest in a pharmacare bill the NDP had tabled and lost in June 2023. Its framework is inherited from the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health's 2016 report: a universal plan that *replaces* existing public and private drug plans, uses Quebec's Régie de l'assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) formulary as the national list, and charges a $5 copayment on brand-name prescriptions with exemptions for people 15 and under, students 16–18, people 65 and over, pregnant women, people with physical disabilities, Employment Insurance recipients and their dependents, and welfare or social assistance recipients and their dependants [3].

On that basis the PBO estimated total drug expenditures under Pharmacare at $33.2 billion in 2024-25 — the assumed first full fiscal year — rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28 [3]. Against a status-quo baseline of $34.6 billion in 2024-25, that is already a small economy-wide saving, and it is the source of the PBO's most counter-intuitive finding: a single payer spends less on drugs in total while spending far more publicly. The mechanism is the transfer of the 40 per cent of prescription spending borne by private insurers and the 14 per cent paid out of pocket into the public column [3].

The cost figures themselves come in three layers, and quoting the wrong one is the most common error in coverage of this file:

- Gross incremental cost to public drug plans: $14.8 billion in 2024-25, rising to $17.3 billion in 2027-28 [3].
- Net incremental cost to the public sector — federal and provincial combined — after accounting for status-quo provincial and direct federal spending and Pharmacare copayment revenues: **$11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28** [3].
- Economy-wide savings on drug expenditures: $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28 [3].

The PBO was explicit that it cannot split the $11.2 billion between Ottawa and the provinces, because no cost-sharing model had been chosen: the incremental cost "could either be borne by the federal government or split between the federal and provincial governments, depending on the cost-sharing model that is ultimately adopted" [3]. Anyone who attributes the $11.2 billion to the federal budget is misreading it.

**Where the savings come from.** The PBO's model attributes economy-wide savings to three channels: negotiating list prices down to the lowest price observed in Canada; extending confidential rebates — assumed at 20 per cent for brand-name drugs and 25 per cent for drugs new to the Canadian market — to the private-insurance and out-of-pocket market, not just the public one; and applying universal generic and biosimilar substitution rules [3]. It assumes a 40 per cent biosimilar share of units after ten years on market, and convergence of generic substitution to the median provincial public plan rate over four years, leaving at most 7 per cent of brand-name drugs with a generic available still dispensed as brand [3].

Against that, it assumes utilization rises 13.5 per cent because patient-borne prices fall by 47 to 100 per cent [3]. That behavioural assumption is doing real work: it is the reason savings are $1.4 billion rather than something larger. And the PBO's own caveat is that "the year-over-year net change is very sensitive to the therapeutic mix of drugs, as well as the pricing effect. Therefore, future drug pricing and market mix will greatly determine the cost of any drug plan" [3].

**The formulary is the whole ballgame.** The PBO costed two alternative drug lists, and they produce radically different answers — which tells you more about the uncertainty in this file than any single point estimate:

- A **catastrophic** formulary, built from drugs accepted by the catastrophic drug programs of British Columbia, Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island between April 2016 and March 2020, gives a net public-sector incremental cost of $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 [3].
- An **essential medicines** formulary based on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines adapted for Canada by researchers at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto gives expenditures $0.4 billion *higher* than the baseline in 2024-25 and $0.3 billion higher in 2027-28 — that is, a small loss rather than a saving, because the list is mostly generics whose prices are already low, so increased utilization is not offset by negotiating gains [3].

So "what pharmacare costs" ranges from roughly $2 billion to $13.4 billion a year depending entirely on which drugs are covered. The $11.2 billion headline is the RAMQ-formulary case, not a universal answer.

**Provincial distribution.** The PBO also found the incremental public cost varies enormously by province relative to what each already spends: from 1.4 times projected baseline public spending in Saskatchewan to nearly three times baseline public spending in Prince Edward Island [3]. That variation reflects differences in existing formularies, utilization, drug mix and prices, and it explains a lot about which provinces found the offer attractive.

**The Act's own costing.** Separately, the PBO costed Bill C-64 itself in a legislative costing note published 15 May 2024, and reached a much smaller number: the first phase would increase federal program spending by **$1.9 billion over five years** [4]. The gap between that and the government's own budget figure of $1.5 billion over five years is what generated the "costs $400 million more than projected" headlines. The two figures are not really in conflict; they rest on different assumptions.

The crucial difference in method is that the C-64 costing models a *top-up*, not a replacement. It assumes any medications currently covered by provincial, territorial and private plans stay covered on the same terms, and that the new program covers the out-of-pocket portion for people who already have coverage plus the full cost for those who have none [4]. It assumes 14 per cent of total prescriptions are not filled for cost-related reasons and that the program picks those up [4]. It assumes no additional confidential rebates, because the program's stated objective was to expand and enhance coverage rather than replace plans [4].

The PBO attached unusually blunt caveats: "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage" [4]. It also excluded behavioural effects such as substitution from unlisted to listed drugs, which it said could raise the total, and excluded savings from fewer Medical Expense Tax Credit claims [4].

The honest summary: $1.9 billion over five years buys a first phase covering two therapeutic areas in the jurisdictions that sign. $11.2 billion a year buys a full single-payer system that replaces private coverage. Neither number is a costing of the program as it actually exists in 2026, because the program as it exists is four bilateral agreements covering contraception and diabetes in four jurisdictions — for which the PBO has published no running cost estimate at all.

q: What does the evidence say about school smartphone bans: which jurisdictions (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states and others) have adopted them, what have evaluations measured about learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong is that evidence?

report.title: School smartphone bans: which jurisdictions adopted them, what evaluations measured on learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong the evidence is
report.body:
## TL;DR

School phone restrictions have spread to 114 education systems — 58% of countries — since 2023, and to Ontario, England, the Netherlands, every Australian state, Quebec, most US states and much of Europe, but they are not one policy: they range from phones kept in bags during lessons to phones collected at the start of the day and held until home time. The strongest causal studies find that restrictions reliably cut in-school phone use and observed classroom disruption, produce average achievement effects near zero with gains concentrated among lower-achieving students and girls, and reduce bullying by roughly 10-18% in the one study using administrative records. Mental-health and cyberbullying effects are mostly null, the argument that a phone's mere presence drains attention fails the best meta-analysis, and the one genuinely randomised trial is in universities, not schools.

## Key Findings

- **Spread.** UNESCO counts 24% of countries with a national school phone ban in June 2023, 40% in early 2025 and 114 systems (58%) by March 2026 [11]. In the US, 39 states have a statewide ban or a rule requiring districts to adopt one [11].
- **Ontario is a lesson-time restriction, not a ban.** PPM 128 (effective 1 September 2024) forbids device use during instructional time except for educator-directed educational purposes, health/medical needs and special education needs, with devices stored out of view; grades 7-12 may use phones at breaks [4]. Enforcement is "spotty" according to end-of-year reporting [28].
- **England went from guidance to statute.** Statutory guidance in force from 29 June 2026, applying from 1 September 2026, requires prohibition "throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [5]. But 99% of English secondary schools already had some restriction, and only 11% had an effective ban [17].
- **The Netherlands began with a sector agreement, not a law:** a "no, unless" rule from 1 January 2024, with 99% of secondary school leaders in line by mid-2025 and 57% using "home or in the vault" [7], [31]. A full statutory ban covering breaks is planned for 1 January 2027 [31].
- **Australia is nine systems with different rules and dates:** Victoria 2020; WA, Tasmania, NSW and SA by term four 2023; Queensland term one 2024 [34], with rules varying from "no possession" in WA primary years to "away during class" in ACT senior years [19].
- **Quebec banned phones in class from January 2024 and everywhere on school grounds including breaks and lunch from the 2025-26 year, citing bullying and violence rather than learning** [30].
- **The best achievement evidence is a precise null.** The national US study of lockable pouches (~5,000 schools, staggered difference-in-differences, nearly 108,000 teacher survey responses) finds a pooled test-score effect of -0.006 school-level SD and rules out improvements larger than about 0.007 student-level SD [13]. High-school maths gains (+0.047 school-level SD, ~0.9 percentile) offset middle-school losses (-0.025 SD) [13], [1].
- **Three studies find gains concentrated at the bottom.** Beland & Murphy (England) found about +0.07 SD on average, driven by the lowest achievers [14]; Beneito & Vicente-Chirivella (Spain) found +10 PISA maths points and +12 science points against a synthetic control [24]; the randomised Indian trial of in-class collection (16,955 students) found +0.086 SD, concentrated among lower-performing, first-year and non-STEM students [26].
- **One study directly contradicts the English estimate.** A replication using all Swedish grade-9 schools found no effect and could reject gains larger than 1% of a standard deviation [15], [16], attributing the divergence to a 76% versus 21% survey response rate and different context [15].
- **Phone use falls sharply under any credible policy.** Teacher-reported in-class personal phone use fell from 61% to 13% in pouch schools [13]; GPS visits fell to about a third of pre-ban levels in the first two months in Florida [3]; in-school phone time fell 0.67 hours in restrictive English schools [32].
- **Students compensate outside school, so total exposure is unchanged.** English students at restrictive schools used phones 0.67 fewer hours in school but showed no difference in weekday, weekend or weekly totals [32], and the harm gradient in that study runs through total use, not in-school use [32].
- **Enforcement costs land first and unevenly.** Florida's ban raised suspensions 12% and in-school suspensions about 20% in year one, with in-school suspensions up roughly 30% for Black students, then the effects disappeared [3]. The pouch study finds incidents up about 15% at adoption, fading and turning negative by year two [13].
- **Bullying evidence leans positive but is thin.** Spanish police-recorded bullying cases fell 9.5-18% among teenagers in treated regions [24]; Norway found bullying down for both genders [35]. South Australia found no difference and slightly higher bullying in the ban group with a baseline imbalance [23]; the pouch study found no improvement in perceived online bullying (-0.039, SE 0.092) [13]; a Flemish total-ban study found no short-term change in cyberbullying victimization [25].
- **Mental health is mostly null.** English cross-section: adjusted wellbeing difference -0.48 on WEMWBS (95% CI -2.05 to 1.06), nothing for anxiety, depression, sleep or activity [32]. Dutch EPoSS: no differences in wellbeing or bullying by ban type, but full bans associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and lower school belonging for girls [18]. The one credible positive is Norwegian: less psychological health-care use among girls [35].
- **Wellbeing may dip before it improves.** The pouch study finds student-reported wellbeing down ~0.2 SD in the adoption year and up 0.16 SD by the second post-adoption year [13].
- **The cognitive rationale is unsupported.** A four-level meta-analysis of 166 effect sizes from 33 studies (4,368 participants) found mere phone presence had no effect on cognitive outcomes, d = -0.02 (95% CI -0.06 to 0.01) [33]. A rule that keeps phones present but out of view has no mechanism to work through except preventing active use.
- **Reviews call the base thin.** Campbell et al.'s pre-registered scoping review found 22 studies, no RCTs, and inconsistent definitions [20]; the LSE review found "remarkably few studies" of policy effects at all [17].
- **Implementation determines effect.** Ontario adherence was associated with lower social media use and lower depression and anxiety symptoms, small-to-medium [29]; self-reported compliance ranged from 63.3% in Flanders [25] to 87% in South Australia [23].
- **No study separates students with ADHD from their peers, and no randomised trial of a school ban exists** [20], [26].

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school phone restrictions, when, and what the rules actually require

School phone restrictions are now the norm across rich democracies, but they are not one policy. They differ on three dimensions that matter for evaluation: what is prohibited (use in class, use anywhere on school grounds, or possession), how long it lasts (lesson time versus the whole day including breaks and lunch), and what legal force it carries (statute, statutory guidance, sector agreement, or school-level discretion). UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report tracks the spread: 24% of countries had a national school phone ban in June 2023, 40% by early 2025, and by March 2026, "114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide" [11]. UNESCO also notes that the bans vary in scope, with many permitting phones for educational purposes, for specific groups of pupils such as those with disabilities or illness, or requiring them only to be switched off and stored away [11]. Some countries do not ban at all but require schools to write their own policies.

### Ontario: instructional-time restriction with escalating consequences

Ontario's instrument is Policy/Program Memorandum 128, reissued 27 June 2024 and effective 1 September 2024, replacing a weaker 2019 version. It is a provincial code-of-conduct standard, not a statute. The core rule: members of the school community must not use personal mobile devices during instructional time except in three circumstances — for educational purposes as directed by an educator, for health and medical purposes, and to support special education needs [4]. "Personal mobile device" is defined broadly to include cellphones, tablets, laptops and smartwatches [4].

The enforcement detail matters more than the headline. For grades 7 to 12, board policy must require that students’ personal mobile devices are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time, except when explicitly permitted [4]. For grade 6 and below, devices must be stored out of view for the full instructional day. If an educator sees a device not stored out of view, "they must require the device be handed in for the instructional period" (grades 7-12) or for the full instructional day (grade 6 and below) [4]. Refusal means being sent to the principal's office, where PPM 145 progressive discipline — including suspension — is available [4]. Boards are separately required to "restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices" [4], and from 2024-25 report cards must comment on classroom distractions, including those related to personal mobile devices [4].

Two features are worth flagging for anyone reading Ontario's policy as a "ban". First, phones are permitted at breaks and lunch for grades 7-12; the restriction is instructional time only, and students retain possession of devices. Second, the Ontario Human Rights Code duty to accommodate means a student with a documented need (which could include some students with ADHD or diabetes monitoring) must be allowed device use regardless [4].

Implementation has been uneven. Reporting at the end of the first school year, the Toronto Star found that "compliance and enforcement has been spotty — and students can still access those sites using personal data" [28]. Where administrators set expectations at the start of the year with assemblies outlining boundaries and consequences, teachers noticed a change in behaviour; where there was no buy-in, phone use remained a daily conflict with little follow-through [28].

### England: from guidance to statute

England's path ran the other way — from permissive to binding. The Department for Education issued non-statutory guidance in February 2024 telling schools to prohibit phone use throughout the day; that guidance has since been made statutory, with the relevant provision in force from 29 June 2026 and the duty applying from 1 September 2026. The current guidance "provides statutory guidance to individual schools and trusts on how to implement a policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [5]. The default is stated flatly: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [5].

Crucially, the English system was already restrictive before any national rule. A 2024 survey of English secondary schools found 11% had an "effective ban" (phones not allowed in school, or stored in lockers or Yondr pouches at the start of the day), 52% had a "ban, but phone present" (phones in bags), 36% had a partial ban (banned in class but allowed at breaks), and no school reported having no ban at all [17]. That distribution is why English evaluations struggle: comparing "ban" to "no ban" there means comparing a large majority to a small, atypically permissive minority.

### The Netherlands: a sector agreement, then a statute

The Netherlands did not legislate first. A national agreement announced in July 2023 set a "no, unless" starting point — phones in class only for educational purposes — from 1 January 2024 for secondary schools, extended to primary and special education from the 2024-25 year. The education ministry's own reasoning was that sector agreements would produce effects "faster and better" than a change in law because ownership stayed closer to schools and teachers [31]. In October 2026 the government reversed course and announced a full legal ban covering lessons and breaks, targeting 1 January 2027, under a "home or in the vault" rule [31].

Compliance with the agreement was near-total on paper: by mid-2025, 99% of secondary school leaders reported policy in line with the national agreement, and more than 57% used a "home or in the vault" policy [7].

### Australian states: nine systems, nine dates

Australia has no national ban; it has eight state and territory systems plus the non-government sector, with different rules and start dates. Victoria banned phones in public primary and secondary schools in 2020; by term four of 2023 Western Australia, Tasmania, New South Wales and South Australia had followed; Queensland restricted phones in term one of 2024 [34]. The rules also differ in strictness: Western Australia's public schools do not permit students in Years K-6 to have a phone in their possession at all, while Years 7-12 may have one but it must be turned off and put away; South Australia's rule is "off and away all day"; the ACT allows no access during the school day for P-10 but only requires phones away during class for Years 11-12; Tasmania and Victoria require phones off and stored [19]. Queensland's rule covers school hours including break times and extends to smartwatches, with exemptions for health, wellbeing and digital learning [19].

New South Wales began its ban in Term 4 2023 and published a one-year review that is a survey of principals rather than an outcome evaluation: 95% of almost 1,000 public school principals supported the ban, 81% said students' learning had improved, 87% said students were less distracted, and 86% said socialising had improved [6]. Those are the perceptions of the people responsible for enforcing the policy, with no comparison group.

### Quebec and the rest of Canada

Quebec moved in two steps. Phone use in class was banned from January 2024; from the start of the 2025-26 school year the ban on phones, earphones and personal mobile devices was extended to the whole school day including breaks and lunch, across the grounds of public and private schools, with exceptions for pedagogical, health and special-needs reasons and application rules set by each school [30]. The government's stated rationale was bullying and violence rather than learning: it said screens are too often the trigger for bullying situations and that, according to the Montreal police, several violent acts originate during class hours [30]. Ontario is the only other province with a province-wide standard; the rest leave it to boards.

### United States: state mandates, district policies

There is no national US ban. As of the UNESCO count, "39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24)" [11]. California's Phone-Free Schools Act, signed in September 2024, is of the second type: it requires every district, charter school and county office of education to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by 1 July 2026, leaving the content to the district — a description drawn from the Governor's press release and the bill text, neither of which I read in full in this pass, so it is flagged rather than relied on. Florida was first, with a statewide requirement in 2023, and it is the state whose ban has been evaluated [3]. The largest US evaluation to date studies lockable pouches, which about 5,000 schools were using by 2026 [13].

### Sweden and France: possession bans

Sweden goes further than most: from autumn 2026 it will be compulsory for all schools and after-school clubs to collect students’ phones and hold them until the end of the day [27]. France legislated in 2018 to ban phone use in schools and collèges and is extending the prohibition to lycées from the 2026 school year; I have not been able to read the French legal texts in full within this pass, so France is named here but not evaluated (see Open questions).

The pattern across jurisdictions is that the word "ban" covers policies ranging from a rule that phones stay in bags during lessons (Ontario grades 7-12, most English schools) to physical collection at the school gate (Sweden from 2026, French lycées from 2026, US pouch schools). Any claim that "bans work" or "bans don't work" is only as precise as the policy it names.

### 2. What evaluations measure on learning and academic achievement — and what they find

This is where the evidence is strongest, most contested, and most often misreported. There are now four credible causal designs on school-age populations, plus one large randomised trial in higher education, and they do not agree.

### The positive results

**England (Beland & Murphy, 2016).** The study that launched the policy wave used a difference-in-differences design on a survey of schools in four English cities (Birmingham, Leicester, London and Manchester), with GCSE exam results as the outcome. Student performance in high-stakes exams rose by about 0.07 standard deviations on average after a ban, and the gains were concentrated among the lowest-achieving students, with no significant impact on high achievers [14]. This is the single most-cited number in the policy literature, and it is genuinely a causal design — but it rests on a 21% survey response rate, covers 2000-2012 (when smartphone ownership and social media use were far lower than now), and treats schools' own autonomous decisions to ban as the source of variation.

**Spain (Beneito & Vicente-Chirivella, 2022).** Two autonomous regions, Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha, banned phones from 2015. Using a synthetic-control comparison, PISA scores in Galicia improved by around 10 points in maths and 12 points in science relative to a synthetic Galicia matched on pre-intervention trends — equivalent to roughly 0.6 to 0.8 years of learning in maths and 0.72 to about one year in science [24], [17]. The authors are careful about what they measured: because the Spanish policy permitted educational use, they frame the estimates not as a response to prohibition of phones per se "but, instead, to the enforcement of using mobile phones for learning purposes only" [24]. The effect was detectable in Galicia and not in Castilla-La Mancha, which the paper does not fully explain.

**Norway (Abrahamsson, 2024/2026).** Using administrative and survey data on Norwegian middle-school smartphone policies with an event-study design, Abrahamsson finds "no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences": bans reduce psychological health-care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls' GPAs and academic-track placement, especially among girls from disadvantaged backgrounds [35]. The paper's earlier discussion-paper version reported the same pattern: girls' GPA improves and their likelihood of attending an academic high-school track increases, with larger effects for low-SES girls [9]. The "no average effect" is not a footnote; it is the headline of the peer-reviewed abstract, and it means the frequently quoted "Norwegian study shows bans work" is only true for girls.

**Florida (Figlio & Özek, 2025/2026).** The first US statewide mandate, studied in one large urban county school district that went further than the state law required, requiring phones silenced and in backpacks for the entire day including lunch and transitions [22]. Comparing schools with high versus low pre-ban in-school phone activity — a design the authors say likely understates effects because all schools were treated [3] — test scores improved in the second year of the ban after an initial adjustment period, with a significant reduction in unexcused absences that "may explain a large fraction of the test score gains" [2]. Magnitudes: test scores up about 0.6 percentile overall in year two, 1.1 percentiles on spring tests, and about 0.9-1.3 percentiles in middle and high school, with no significant effect for female or elementary students [3]. Average daily smartphone visits dropped to about one-third of pre-ban levels in the first two months, with no comparable change at other county locations [3].

**Higher education, randomised (Sungu, Choudhury & Bjerre-Nielsen, 2025).** The cleanest design in the literature is not in a school: a cluster-randomised trial across 10 higher-education institutions in India, with 16,955 students in Spring 2024, randomising department-semesters to mandatory in-class phone deposit. Grades rose by 0.086 standard deviations on average (95% CI 0.015 to 0.157), with the largest effects among lower-performing, first-year and non-STEM students [26]. The authors state the limit plainly: the study was conducted in higher-education institutions where students are already academically selected, and effects might be more pronounced at lower grade levels — an avenue for future research [26].

### The null results

**Sweden (Kessel, Hardardottir & Tyrefors, 2020).** A deliberate partial replication of Beland & Murphy using all Swedish grade-9 schools, with a 76% survey response rate (1,086 of 1,423 schools) and 16,724 school-year observations, found no impact of school phone bans on merit points, national maths test scores or the share of students failing. Their conclusion: "In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" [15]. With the socioeconomic index included they can reject positive effects larger than 1% of a standard deviation, and the treatment effect is never significant at the 5% level [16]. The point estimates for merit points are slightly negative (-0.034 to -0.042) and never significant. Because their confidence intervals exclude the Beland-Murphy magnitude, the two studies are in direct statistical conflict: this is not a case where different contexts allow both results to stand as equally good evidence for the same policy.

**The largest US study (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow & Jacob, 2026).** The national evaluation of lockable pouches covers nearly 5,000 schools and uses a staggered difference-in-differences design with teacher survey data from nearly 108,000 responses covering about half of US middle and high schools [13]. Its achievement finding is a precise null: in the pooled middle-and-high-school sample the estimated effect on the combined test-score index is -0.006 school-level standard deviations (SE 0.010), approximately -0.003 student-level SD, and "the precision of the estimates allows us to rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" [13]. The heterogeneity cuts both ways: high schools see modest positive effects, particularly in maths (0.047 school-level SD, about 0.024 student SD or roughly 0.9 percentile), while middle schools see small negative effects (combined -0.025 SD) [13], [1]. If any school-level phone policy were going to move test scores in the US, physically locking phones in pouches for the whole day is the strongest version of it — and it did not.

**England (SMART Schools, 2025).** The cross-sectional comparison of 30 English secondary schools (20 restrictive, 10 permissive; 1,227 students aged 12-15) found no evidence of a difference in English or maths attainment between policy types (English adjusted odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 0.85-2.47; maths 1.01, 0.45-2.27) [32]. Even the sensitivity analysis restricted to the four schools where phones were genuinely inaccessible found no significant differences on any outcome [32]. Note the ceiling on what this design can detect: with only 10 permissive schools in the sample and a school-level response rate of 8.73% and 10.42% respectively [32], it is not powered to find small effects — but its null is consistent with the pouch null rather than with Beland & Murphy.

**PISA 2022 (Kemp et al., 2024).** An initial analysis suggested phone restrictions reduced distraction, but once social class, gender and behaviour were controlled for, students in schools with smartphone restrictions had lower achievement across PISA test scores than schools that permitted phone use — though effect sizes were low in all models [17]. This is a cross-country observational comparison and cannot establish direction: schools serving disadvantaged intakes may be more likely to restrict.

### How to reconcile them

Three explanations do real work, and they are not mutually exclusive.

*What is being compared.* In the pouch study, roughly 62% of adopting schools previously operated a "no-show" regime (phones allowed in bags but out of sight) and 23% had no formal phone policy at all, while only about 1-5% of comparison schools adopted similarly strict alternatives in 2023-2025 [13]. So the pouch study compares a genuine tightening against a largely untreated control. In England, by contrast, 99% of secondary schools already had some restriction before the 2024 guidance [17], and in the SMART Schools frame 1,245 of 1,341 state secondary schools had restrictive policies [32]. Beland & Murphy were comparing schools that banned with schools that did not, in an era when most did not.

*Who benefits.* The consistent positive finding across Beland & Murphy, Beneito & Vicente-Chirivella, Abrahamsson and Sungu et al. is that gains concentrate in lower-achieving, lower-SES or first-year students and in girls, not in the average. A policy that helps the bottom tercile and does nothing for the top will show a near-zero average — which is exactly the pattern in the pouch study, where high-school maths gains and middle-school losses nearly cancel.

*What the outcome measures.* GCSE and PISA measure accumulated learning over years; US state tests in the pouch study's districts may be less sensitive or less well aligned to the school year in which the change occurred. The pouch study's own authors note that their phone-use decline (about 80% in teacher reports of in-class personal use, from 61% to 13%) was much larger than the GPS-measured decline, which they treat as a conservative lower bound [13] — so the null is not plausibly explained by failed implementation.

My inference, labelled as such: the best reading of this literature is that a school phone restriction produces small achievement gains at most, concentrated among lower-achieving students, and that the gains are largest where the counterfactual involves substantial in-school phone use by those students (England pre-2012, Spain 2015, Norway's girls, first-year university students in India). Where phones were already largely out of classrooms, or where students' total exposure is unaffected, the measurable learning effect is close to zero.

### 3. Attention, classroom disruption, discipline and phone use itself

Attention is the outcome that motivates most bans and the one that is hardest to measure well. The evidence splits cleanly into what phone use in classrooms does to attention, and what removing phones does.

### Phone use in class is a large, teacher-reported problem

In the US, 72% of high-school teachers say students being distracted by cellphones is a major problem in their classroom, compared with 33% of middle-school teachers and 6% of elementary teachers — a Pew Research Center survey of more than 2,500 public-school teachers, cited in the pouch study's own framing [13]. That is a measure of teacher perception, not of attention, but it establishes that the perceived problem is concentrated in high school, which is exactly where the pouch study finds its small positive maths effects.

### Removing phones does cut in-school phone use, and everyone agrees on that

Every evaluation that measured phone use found the policy reduced it in school.

The pouch study is the strongest evidence on this point because it uses two independent measures. Teacher reports indicate the share of students using phones in class for personal reasons fell from 61% to 13% after adoption, "a drop of roughly 80 percent", substantially larger than the decline in non-adopting schools [13]. GPS data from a subset of students shows average daily smartphone visits fell to about one-third of pre-ban levels in the first two months of the Florida district's ban, with no comparable change at other locations in the county [3]. The pouch paper treats the GPS decline of roughly 30% by the third year as a conservative lower bound [13].

In England, the SMART Schools study quantified the reduction in hours rather than percentages: students at restrictive schools had lower phone time during school by 0.67 hours (95% CI -0.92 to -0.43) and lower in-school social media time by 0.54 hours (95% CI -0.74 to -0.36) [32]. The English study's important qualification is that this did not translate into lower total use: there was no evidence of differences in weekday, weekend or weekly totals [32]. Students appear to make up the time outside school.

In South Australia, 87% of students in ban schools reported complying with the ban at the first time point, with compliance lower among older students, frequent social media posters, prior in-school phone users and students who had experienced bullying [23]. In Flanders, by the final wave of a total-ban study only 63.3% of students reported adhering, which the authors say indicates the intervention was implemented but also that a substantial share of students did not fully comply [25].

### On-task behaviour and classroom disruption: observed improvements, self-reports that disagree

The randomised trial in Indian higher education collected classroom observation data alongside grades, and the results are the most interesting in the literature because observers and students diverged. Spot checks found fewer instances of student chatter and disruptive behaviour, along with reduced phone usage and increased engagement among teachers — a classroom environment more conducive to learning. But the same spot checks found that "students appear more distracted, possibly due to withdrawal from habitual phone checking, yet, students did not report being more distracted" [26]. The authors describe this as a distraction paradox: removing the object of distraction increased visible restlessness without increasing felt distraction.

The pouch study's measure of attention points the other way — or rather, nowhere. It found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention" [1], with a point estimate on classroom attention of -0.088 (SE 0.085), which the authors read as no evidence of change following adoption [13]. They caution that this measure has pre-trend problems, so the null is not decisive. Note the distinction: observers in India saw less disruption and more teacher engagement, while self-reported attention in the US did not move. If the policy's real effect is on the classroom environment rather than on students' experienced attention, self-report instruments will miss it.

### Discipline: a real short-run cost, unevenly borne

Both major US studies find that enforcement itself creates disruption before it reduces it, and that the cost falls disproportionately on Black students.

In Florida, the ban increased disciplinary incidents and suspensions in the first year by 12% of the comparison-group mean and in-school suspensions by about 20%; the effects disappeared in the second year, and there were no significant effects on out-of-school suspensions. The first-year effects were driven mostly by Black students: in-school suspensions rose roughly 30% for Black students with no significant effect for White and Hispanic students [3]. The authors interpret the pattern as an adjustment period ending in a new steady state [2].

The pouch study found the same shape with a different measure: disciplinary incidents increased in the year of implementation by about 0.03 student-level standard deviations — corresponding to roughly a 15% increase in suspension rates — and the effect fades in subsequent years [13]. At the adoption date the estimate is larger (0.078 school-level SD, about 15% above baseline), moves toward zero in the following year, and turns negative by the second year after adoption [13].

The equity finding is the one that deserves the most weight in policy terms and receives the least attention. A rule whose first-year cost is a 30% rise in in-school suspensions for Black students, which then dissipates as students and staff adapt, is a rule that imposes a transitional harm on a specific group — and neither the pouch study nor the Florida study can rule out that the adaptation is to the punishment rather than to the rule.

### The mechanism question: does a phone in the room drain attention?

The strongest theoretical argument for removing phones from classrooms — that the mere presence of a phone consumes cognitive resources, the "brain drain" effect — does not survive the best synthesis. A four-level meta-analysis pooling 166 effect sizes from 53 samples and 33 studies with 4,368 participants found that "the mere presence of smartphone had no significant effect on cognitive outcomes (d = −0.02, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.01], p = .246)", and the effect was not moderated by demographics, smartphone dependency or how presence was manipulated [33].

That null matters for how bans are justified. If a phone sitting in a bag or pocket does not itself degrade working memory or sustained attention, then a policy that requires phones to be stored out of view but present (Ontario grades 7-12, most English schools) has no cognitive mechanism to work through — it can only work by preventing active use. Policies that physically remove devices (pouches, collection at the gate) remove active use and nothing more. The meta-analysis is about mere presence in laboratory tasks, not about a student checking Instagram under a desk, so it does not show that phone use is harmless; it shows that the "even having it there hurts" rationale is unsupported.

### What this adds up to

The consistent, well-measured findings on attention and disruption are: in-school phone use falls sharply under any credible policy; observed classroom disruption and off-task chatter fall; self-reported attention and perceived distraction do not reliably improve; discipline incidents rise in the first year and then fall back; and students compensate for in-school reductions with out-of-school use. The gap between observed and self-reported attention is unresolved and, in my reading, the most under-studied outcome in this literature.

### 4. Bullying, cyberbullying, mental health and well-being

Bullying and mental health are the outcomes that actually justify the political urgency behind these policies — Quebec's government cited screens as the trigger for bullying and cited police reports of violence beginning during class hours [30] — and they are where the evidence is most contradictory. The honest summary is that bullying results lean positive but rest on aggregate administrative data, and mental-health results are mostly null except for one well-identified Norwegian finding about girls' health-care use.

### Bullying: the positive findings

**Spain.** Beneito & Vicente-Chirivella is the only study that measures bullying directly with administrative records across a policy change. Using police-reported bullying cases per 10,000 students from 2012 to 2017, they find that "bullying incidence fell by around 9.5% to 18% over its pre-intervention levels among teenagers in the treated regions" [24]. King et al. summarise the same paper as showing a 15-18% reduction in bullying incidence among students aged 12-17, and 10-18% among 15-17 year-olds [23]. The design uses under-12s as a placebo group, which is a genuine strength: if the effect were a regional trend rather than the phone ban, younger children (not covered by the policy) would move too.

**Norway.** Abrahamsson finds that post-ban bullying among both genders decreases, alongside reduced psychological health-care use among girls [9], [35]. The measure is school-level bullying reported in the national student survey, with annual data points. Vereecke et al. criticise exactly this: adherence and consistency of implementation across schools remain unclear, bullying was measured via school-level averages limiting insight into within-school variation, and the design included only annual data points from 2010-2018 without measurements immediately preceding the ban, preventing assessment of short-term effects [25]. That is a fair critique of precision, though it does not invalidate the finding.

### Bullying: the null and negative findings

**South Australia (King et al., 2024).** A preregistered natural experiment across five public secondary schools, using a 2x2 repeated-measures design with 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up one month later, found that ban and no-ban groups "did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging. There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [23]. The authors also report a baseline imbalance: contrary to predictions, the no-ban group reported significantly greater academic engagement and lower bullying at baseline, though the effect was small [23]. A study that compares schools which chose different policies is comparing schools that differ in other ways too.

**The pouch study.** It found no clear evidence of improvements in perceived online bullying, with an estimate of -0.039 (SE 0.092) on the perceived online bullying measure — small and insignificant [1], [13].

**Flanders (Vereecke et al., 2026).** The best-designed short-run study of a total ban — 960 students, eight waves across one academic year, one pre-ban wave and seven monthly post-ban waves — found that "No short-term changes emerged in social loneliness, friend support, or cyberbullying victimization, although cyberbullying perpetration declined slightly. Over time, social loneliness increased modestly, friend support remained stable, and cyberbullying fluctuated at low levels" [25]. The perpetration decline is the one positive signal, and it is small.

**Older studies.** Two older studies found cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place (Davis & Koepke, 2016; Walker, 2013), as the EPoSS authors note [18]. Those are cross-sectional and predate smartphone saturation, so they are weak evidence — but they are evidence against, and they are rarely cited.

**The measurement problem underneath all of this.** A 2019 Australian study found that 99% of students who were cyberbullied were also bullied face-to-face. If that is right, a school-hours phone ban cannot reach most bullying, because most bullying has an in-person component that continues regardless. The Spanish result is compatible with this: a 9.5-18% reduction is meaningful but leaves the large majority of cases untouched.

### Mental health: mostly null, with one credible exception

**England (SMART Schools).** In 1,227 students across 30 schools, mean mental wellbeing (WEMWBS) was 47 with "no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)", and there was no difference in anxiety, depression, sleep, physical activity, attainment or disruptive classroom behaviour [32]. The study did find a dose-response in total use: increases in smartphone and social media time were associated with reduced mental wellbeing on weekdays, weekends and across the week, although in-school phone and social media use was not significantly associated with outcomes [32]. That is the crucial finding for the policy question. The harm signal lives in total exposure, and restrictive school policies did not reduce total exposure — in-school phone time was 0.67 hours lower but weekday, weekend and weekly totals showed no evidence of difference [32].

**The pouch study.** Student-reported subjective well-being declined in the year of adoption and then rebounded: a decline of roughly 0.2 student-level standard deviations followed by an increase of 0.16 SD, becoming positive by the second post-adoption year [13]. The authors are appropriately cautious, reading it as suggestive evidence of adjustment costs followed by adaptation. For scale, the paper compares it to the effect of deactivating Facebook for four weeks. A 0.16 SD improvement is small but not trivial; a 0.2 SD decline in the first year is a real cost borne by the cohort that experiences the transition.

**The Netherlands (EPoSS).** The Dutch study compared 1,398 secondary students in 24 schools (9 partial-ban, 15 full-ban) surveyed between September 2024 and February 2025. "No significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes. However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [18]. This is cross-sectional, so it cannot establish direction — schools with worse climates might adopt full bans — but it is the only study that finds a negative association, and it is on outcomes (belonging, connectedness) that the other studies do not measure.

**Norway.** The single credible positive mental-health finding: bans reduce psychological health-care use among girls [35]. This is administrative data on actual service use, not self-reported symptoms, which makes it stronger than most well-being measures in this literature — a reduction in GP consultations for psychological symptoms is costly to fake and hard to attribute to response bias. It is also specific: no average effect on mental health, no effect for boys.

**Ontario.** A study of more than 600 children and young adults aged 6-18 from a pandemic-era longitudinal cohort, published in the Canadian Journal of Psychiatry, found that greater adherence to Ontario's cellphone restrictions was associated with lower social media use and, in turn, lower symptoms of depression and anxiety, with a small-to-medium effect size. The lead author's own summary of the policy implication is about implementation: "It’s not sufficient just to have the policies. We need to help educators with how to implement them in schools so they can be effective" [29]. Note the design: this measures adherence, not policy adoption, so it identifies the effect of students actually following the rule — a selected group — rather than the effect of the rule.

**South Australia (Radunz et al., 2025).** A preregistered 2x2 repeated-measures study across five schools, 1,319 students at baseline and 603 (45.7%) at follow-up, found that no significant differences in mental health outcomes were found between ban and no-ban groups based on social media posting levels [21]. The follow-up was in early Term 3 of 2023, only weeks after the ban began [21], which is far too soon for a mental-health effect to plausibly emerge. What the study did find is more informative for policy design: frequent posters had higher distress (d = -0.29), more self-harm thoughts (d = -0.47) and more self-harm behaviours (d = -0.60) [21]. The concentration of harm in heavy users is consistent with the English total-exposure finding.

**Higher education.** In the randomised Indian trial there were no aggregate effects on average phone-use time, the frequency with which students bring phones to school, or online harassment [26]. Note that this is a classroom-only collection policy in universities, the weakest form of restriction.

### Why the mental-health results come out null

Three structural reasons, each supported by the studies themselves.

First, the mechanism is not engaged. A ban reduces in-school exposure by roughly half an hour to an hour but leaves total daily exposure unchanged [32], and the dose-response harm sits in total exposure [32]. Students in England reported average smartphone use of 4-6 hours per day across both policy types [12], so an hour in school is a small share.

Second, the outcome is rare. In the South Australian sample, problematic phone use was reported by 2.6% of students [23]. A policy cannot produce a large population-level mental-health effect on an outcome with a 2.6% base rate unless it is extraordinarily effective for that small group — and if it is, mean-level studies will not detect it.

Third, the timing is wrong. The studies with the shortest follow-ups (weeks) find nothing [21], the study with three years of follow-up finds a decline followed by a rebound [13], and the study with eight monthly waves finds modest increases in loneliness rather than improvements [25]. Whatever effect exists appears to be slow, dynamic and possibly non-monotonic.

My inference: the mental-health case for school bans is currently weaker than the bullying case, and both are weaker than the political rhetoric suggests. The one finding that would justify a targeted policy — reduced psychological health-care use among girls in Norway [35] — has not been replicated anywhere, and the studies best placed to replicate it (the English cross-section, the US pouch study, the Dutch EPoSS study) found nothing for well-being overall.

### 5. How strong the evidence is: designs, identification problems, compliance, and where the reviews disagree

The literature is better than it was five years ago and still weaker than the confidence of the policy debate. What follows separates the design problems that genuinely limit what can be concluded from the ones that are routinely overstated.

### The designs, ranked

**Randomised controlled trials: one, and not in a school.** The Indian higher-education trial randomising 16,955 students across 10 institutions to mandatory in-class phone deposit is the only RCT in this area [26]. It is a good trial of a narrow policy (collection during class, adults, one semester) and its authors are explicit that generalisation to lower grades and to countries where students carry other devices is untested [26]. Every other causal claim in this literature is quasi-experimental.

**Difference-in-differences and event studies with administrative outcomes.** These are the strongest school-age designs: Florida (Figlio & Özek), Norway (Abrahamsson), and the national pouch study (Allcott et al.). Each has a defensible counterfactual, large samples, and outcomes not self-reported by the people who implemented the policy. Their weaknesses are different from each other:

- Florida compares high- versus low-pre-ban-phone-use schools within a district where all schools were treated, which the authors say likely understates effects [3]. That means the reported 0.6-1.1 percentile test-score gain is a lower bound under their assumptions — but it also means the estimate is identified off within-district variation in phone use, not off the ban itself.
- Norway's event study has annual data points and no measurement immediately preceding the ban, which Vereecke et al. note prevents assessment of short-term effects [25].
- The pouch study's identifying assumption is that adopting and non-adopting schools would have followed parallel trends. Its treatment contrast is strong (62% of adopters previously had a "no-show" regime, 23% no formal policy at all, while only about 1-5% of comparison schools adopted similarly strict alternatives in 2023-2025) [13]. Its weakness is measurement of the outcome: US state test scores in a staggered adoption window with pandemic-era disruptions.

**Cross-sectional comparisons of differently-policied schools.** SMART Schools in England and EPoSS in the Netherlands are the two large examples, and both are weaker than they look. SMART Schools has 10 permissive schools against 20 restrictive, in a national frame where only 96 of 1,341 state secondary schools were permissive, with school-level response rates of 8.73% and 10.42% [32]. It also found that of its 20 "restrictive" schools, 16 merely required phones off in bags — only 4 made phones genuinely inaccessible, and a sensitivity analysis on those 4 found no significant differences on any outcome [32]. EPoSS compares 24 schools, with 9 partial-ban and 15 full-ban, in a single cross-section [18]. Neither can rule out that schools choose policies that match their intake.

**Perception surveys by the implementing authority.** The NSW one-year review (95% of principals support the ban, 81% say learning improved) [6], the Dutch government-commissioned monitoring (75% of secondary schools report easier concentration, 59% a better social environment, 28% improved results) [8], and South Australia's departmental claims (a 63% decline in "critical incidents involving social media") [19] are not evaluations in any useful sense. They measure what the people responsible for the policy believe happened, with no counterfactual. The Dutch government's own monitoring is more candid than most: it reports positive effects on concentration, well-being and classroom climate but says it is too early to say anything about effects on learning performance [7].

**Reviews.** Two systematic reviews bracket the field. Campbell et al. (2024), a pre-registered PRISMA-ScR scoping review, found 22 studies meeting inclusion criteria and concluded: "We found an absence of randomized controlled trials with evidence resting on a small number of studies with different designs, samples, operational definitions of mobile phone bans (i.e. partial, or complete bans) and outcome measures, making reconciliation of findings challenging" [20]. The Digital Futures for Children review at LSE (Rahali, Kidron & Livingstone, 2024) put it more bluntly: despite considerable media attention, remarkably few studies have examined the effects of school smartphone policies on students’ academic performance or other outcomes [17].

### The word "ban" is doing damage

The most consequential methodological problem is definitional. The LSE review notes that despite the word ‘ban’ being widely employed, school smartphone policies vary considerably in content and implementation, and that few, if any, schools have implemented outright bans [17]. This is not pedantry. In England, 11% of secondary schools had an effective ban and 52% had a "ban, but phone present" [17]. In the SMART Schools sample, 16 of 20 "restrictive" schools left phones accessible in bags [32]. In Ontario, phones are permitted at breaks for grades 7-12 [4]. Sweden from 2026 collects phones at the start of the day [27]. These policies cannot plausibly have the same effect, and studies that pool them under "ban" will produce estimates that are averages over very different treatments — usually biased toward zero, because most "bans" are partial.

### The compliance and implementation problem

Compliance is measurable and varies enormously. The pouch study found teacher-reported in-class personal phone use fell from 61% to 13% [13]. In South Australia 87% of students in ban schools reported complying [23]. In Flanders, a total ban achieved 63.3% self-reported adherence by the final wave, which the authors read as evidence of implementation plus a substantial non-compliant minority [25]. In Ontario, reporting at the end of the first year found enforcement "spotty" and students reaching social media over personal data [28]; where administrators set clear expectations, teachers noticed behaviour change, and where they did not, phone use remained a constant conflict [28].

The Ontario adherence study is the cleanest demonstration that this matters for outcomes: greater adherence was associated with lower social media use and, in turn, lower depression and anxiety symptoms, small-to-medium in size [29]. If the effect of a policy depends on adherence, then studies that ignore implementation are estimating the effect of announcing a rule, not of changing behaviour.

### Where the credible studies genuinely conflict

Three conflicts cannot be resolved by context-shopping, and any honest account has to state them.

1. **Beland & Murphy (England, +0.07 SD) versus Kessel et al. (Sweden, null with confidence intervals excluding +0.07).** Kessel et al. ran a deliberate replication and attribute the divergence to design (76% survey response versus 21%) and context (Swedish teachers may already have restricted phones in practice; Sweden is unusually computer-dense) [15], [16]. The LSE review adds a third consideration: Beland & Murphy's data cover a period "when smartphone ownership was lower and social media was less prevalent" [17]. My reading: the Swedish study is the better-designed test of the same proposition, and the English estimate should not be treated as a current effect size.

2. **Florida (+0.6 to 1.1 percentiles) versus the national pouch study (-0.003 student SD, ruling out >0.007).** Both are US difference-in-differences studies of strict policies. The plausible reconciliation is heterogeneity: the pouch study finds high-school maths gains (0.047 school-level SD) offset by middle-school losses (-0.025 SD) [13], and Florida's district may be atypical. The national study's near-zero average is the better estimate of the average effect; Florida's is the better estimate of what a well-implemented strict policy in a high-phone-use district can do. Neither is a good estimate of the other.

3. **Spain (+10 PISA maths points, 9.5-18% less bullying) versus England (no attainment or bullying difference) and the Netherlands (no well-being or bullying difference).** Spain used regional policy variation with a synthetic control; England and the Netherlands used cross-sections of schools that chose their own policies. The Spanish design is stronger for causal inference; the English and Dutch findings are stronger for describing what current policies in those countries deliver. Both can be true if Spanish schools in 2015 had much more in-school phone use to remove than English schools in 2023-24.

### What the evidence can and cannot support

Supported with high confidence: school restrictions substantially reduce in-school phone use; observed classroom disruption falls; enforcement produces a first-year rise in disciplinary incidents that disproportionately affects Black students in the US and then fades; students compensate with out-of-school use, so total exposure is largely unchanged; and the "mere presence of a phone" cognitive-drain mechanism is not supported by the best meta-analysis (d = -0.02) [33].

Supported with moderate confidence: small average achievement effects near zero, with gains concentrated among lower-achieving students and girls, and larger effects where pre-policy in-school phone use was high; bullying reductions of roughly 10-18% in the one administrative-data study [24]; a possible reduction in girls' psychological health-care use in Norway [35].

Not supported by any adequate evidence: that bans improve average mental health or well-being; that they reduce cyberbullying in the short run; that they raise attainment for typical students; and that the effect sizes claimed in advocacy literature (large gains for all students) survive contact with the better-designed studies.

A standing problem with the whole field: nearly every study is of a policy adopted by schools or regions that chose to adopt it, at a moment when adoption was becoming socially desirable. The one randomised trial is in universities. There is still no randomised trial of a school phone ban, and the reviews say so explicitly [20].

One further caution on the record itself. Advocacy organisations on both sides produce literature reviews that select consistent studies: the Paragon Institute's review concludes bans reliably help disadvantaged students, while Haidt and Rausch's collaborative review at NYU Stern organises the same literature toward a stronger pro-restriction conclusion. Neither is peer-reviewed. The peer-reviewed reviews — Campbell et al. and the LSE review — both emphasise how thin and heterogeneous the base is [20], [17].


## Open questions

**Nobody has run a randomised trial of a school phone ban.** Campbell et al. state the absence explicitly [20], and it remains true: the only RCT in this area is the Indian higher-education trial of in-class collection [26]. Every school-level causal claim rests on policies adopted by schools, districts or regions that chose to adopt them, at a moment when adoption was becoming normatively expected. That is a real threat to identification in a way that parallel-trends tests cannot fully address.

**No study has measured the outcome that matters most for the ADHD and attention question.** Nothing in this literature separates students with ADHD or other attention-regulation differences from their peers. Given that Ontario's PPM 128 explicitly permits device use "to support special education needs" [4], and given that the population most likely to be harmed by a phone in the room is also the population most likely to have an accommodation, the net effect for those students is unknown. This is the clearest gap in the whole field and it is not being filled.

**The observer/self-report divergence is unresolved.** The Indian trial found fewer disruptions observed but no increase in students' felt attention [26]; the US pouch study found no improvement in self-reported classroom attention [13]. Whether a ban improves the classroom environment without improving students' experience of attention — and what that means for learning — has not been tested in a school-age sample with both instruments.

**Total exposure is unmeasured in most studies.** SMART Schools found that students compensate for in-school reductions outside school, leaving total use unchanged [32]. Only that study and the pouch study attempt to measure total use. If harm scales with total exposure [32] and bans do not shift total exposure, then the mental-health rationale for a school-only ban is theoretically weak — but nobody has tested a policy that pairs an in-school ban with an out-of-school component.

**Bullying measurement is aggregate or absent.** The Spanish administrative series is the strongest measure [24]; Norway's is school-level annual [25]; South Australia's short-run studies found no difference [23], [21]. Nobody has linked school phone policy to individual-level bullying reports across a policy change. The claim that bans reduce cyberbullying therefore rests on one regional study of police-recorded cases.

**Long-run effects beyond three years are unknown.** The pouch study covers three years and finds well-being turning positive by year two [13]; the Flemish study covers eight months [25]; the Norwegian data are annual to 2018 [35]. Whether the initial discipline spike and well-being dip [13], [3] produce lasting harm for the affected cohort has not been studied.

**Implementation is not standardised or measured in most evaluations.** Adherence ranges from 63.3% [25] to 87% [23] to an 80% drop in teacher-reported in-class use [13], and only the Ontario adherence study treats adherence as the exposure of interest [29]. A field that reports "the effect of a ban" without measuring whether the ban happened is reporting the effect of an announcement.

**Where coverage in this report is thin, and what I found but could not read.** The reading allowance for this pass ran out before I could open several primary documents I had identified. Chris can reply "keep going" and I will fetch and note them:

- *France.* A French Senate written answer (2025) reportedly describes the "pause numérique" experiment in around 200 collèges from the 2024 school year as showing improved school climate, calmer relations, better attention and more social interaction, with close to 80% of participating collèges reporting positively; a separate February 2025 report on an evaluation says the phone ban had no effect on grades or behaviour. These two accounts conflict and neither has been read in full here, so France is named in this report but not evaluated. The Ministry of Education page confirms the extension of the ban to lycées from the 2026 school year.
- *Netherlands.* The primary source behind the Dutch figures is the Kohnstamm Instituut / Oberon final monitoring report and factsheet published by Rijksoverheid on 3 July 2025. I read a secondary summary [7], [8] but not the report, which may contain the second measurement and any attainment data.
- *Ontario.* EQAO provincial assessment results for 2024-25 (released 3 December 2025) and 2025-26 (released September 2026) exist and are published, but no published evaluation links them to PPM 128. Using them to judge the ban would be an uncontrolled before/after comparison confounded by pandemic recovery, curriculum changes and tutoring funding; I would not present such a comparison as evidence about phones.
- *New South Wales.* The only published evaluation is the principal survey [6]; the CESE literature review from 2018 is candid that the evidence is mixed and that students are adept at getting around bans [10]. I found no outcome-based NSW evaluation.
- *US state-level attainment and California.* I found no study using state accountability data across multiple states' bans; the pouch study is the closest. California's Phone-Free Schools Act was signed in September 2024 and, according to the Governor's press release and the bill text as described in search results, requires every district, charter school and county office of education to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by 1 July 2026, leaving the content to the district. I did not read the statute or the release in full, so treat that description as unverified here.

## Beyond this question

For anyone deciding policy, three implications follow from the evidence rather than from the advocacy on either side.

*Specify the policy, not the slogan.* The measured effects differ by whether phones are in bags, in lockers, in pouches, or at home, and by whether the restriction covers breaks. Ontario's instructional-time rule with devices in students' possession [4] is a fundamentally different intervention from Sweden's collection at the start of the day [27], and the evaluations that find near-zero effects are mostly evaluations of the weaker version [32], [17]. If a jurisdiction wants an effect size, it has to buy the treatment: physical separation, all day, enforced.

*Budget for the first-year cost and for who bears it.* Both US studies find disciplinary incidents rise in year one and fall back, with a disproportionate rise in in-school suspensions for Black students — roughly 30% in Florida [3], about 15% higher suspension rates nationally at adoption [13]. A policy justified by equity that produces a transitional equity harm needs an explicit implementation plan, not a press release.

*Expect effects at the bottom, not the middle.* The positive findings across England, Spain, Norway and India concentrate in lower-achieving, lower-SES, first-year and female students [14], [24], [35], [26]. The right evaluation design for a school ban is therefore subgroup-first: measuring the average and reporting a null will miss the effect the policy was supposed to have, and reporting an average gain will overstate what most students get.

For researchers, the field's binding constraint is not more difference-in-differences studies of policies that were adopted voluntarily. It is (a) a randomised or encouragement-design trial in schools, (b) individual-level bullying and mental-health outcomes measured across a policy change with adherence measured, and (c) any evidence at all on students with ADHD and other attention-regulation differences.
