q: Write an article from the record's research on whether banning or restricting Airbnb and other short-term rentals actually improved housing in Canadian cities. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: Short-term rental bans in Hamilton, Toronto and Vancouver: the units that returned, the neighbourhoods that gained, and the rent falls that came from new construction
report.body:
Canadian cities restricted short-term rentals to bring homes back to renters. The rules returned housing in dense downtown blocks where commercial operators had concentrated, and did little to city-wide rents, which moved with construction and interest rates.

## The promise was homes returned, not listings removed

Hamilton's council passed its bylaw in January 2023 with a number in mind: <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="Executive summary">The stated goal was to return roughly 650 family-sized units to long-term inventory.</q> The rule it wrote was strict. <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§1">STRs are permitted only in a host's principal residence</q>, with a single licence per operator, a <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§1">28-night cap on a single stay</q>, inspections, and <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§1">Provincial Offences Act fines up to $100,000 per offence</q>. Toronto and Vancouver had passed principal-residence rules earlier, and British Columbia applied one province-wide in 2024.

The case for all of them rested on a chain of assumptions: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Executive summary">that STRs significantly reduce long-term housing supply, that banning them returns those units to the long-term rental (LTR) market, and that this added supply lowers rents</q>. Every link had to hold before a bylaw could pull a rent down. A review of the Canadian and international evidence concluded that <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Executive summary">each link in this chain is weaker than political messaging suggested</q>.

## The stock was too small for a city-wide effect

Statistics Canada counted the short-term units listed long enough that they could plausibly serve as long-term homes. They <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">accounted for less than 0.5% of housing units in Canada's five largest CMAs in 2021</q>, and <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">Vancouver had the highest big-city share at 0.45%</q>. In Hamilton the whole market was small: <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§4">The 1,250 listings represented roughly 0.5% of Hamilton's total housing stock</q>.

The Conference Board of Canada then tested the rent link directly, using Airbnb's booking data and federal rent data across <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">330 Canadian neighbourhoods</q>. Of the <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">roughly 30% increase in rents observed across Canadian neighbourhoods between 2016 and 2022, at most less than one percentage point</q> could be attributed to Airbnb activity. Its summary was flat: <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§3b">We find no compelling evidence that the level of Airbnb activity had a meaningful impact on rents.</q>

The comparison between cities cut the same way, and against the policy. Cities that had already restricted short-term rentals were not cheaper afterwards: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">municipalities that had already imposed principal-residence restrictions did not subsequently exhibit lower rents</q> than comparable cities without them. The likelier reading is that <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">these cities adopted the policies because they were already in housing stress, not that the policies caused affordability</q>.

Scale is the reason. Against a shortage counted in the hundreds of thousands of homes, <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 8">The arithmetic does not work: <0.5% of stock cannot offset a deficit measured in hundreds of thousands of units.</q>

## Where the rules did return housing

There is a real effect here, and it is worth naming precisely, because it is the part of the policy a city can defend. In the densest parts of the three big markets, commercial operators <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 8">were genuinely removing housing from the long-term market and contributing measurably (though modestly) to local rent pressure</q>. Vancouver's task force put a number on the return: about <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 2">2,700 units returned to the long-term market</q> in the two years after its stricter rules.

What the best-designed studies isolate is the commercial operator, not the spare room. In Berlin, <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 3">each additional commercial Airbnb listing displaces 0.23–0.37 rental units; non-commercial restrictions had no measurable effect</q>. A bylaw aimed at people running several units in one building is aimed at the thing that moves housing. The same bylaw aimed at the whole city's rent index is not.

## Most of the listings removed were not homes returned

New York ran the largest test, taking listings from about 22,000 to about 6,800. Its enforcement office confirmed roughly 1,400 conversions to long-term leases, which means <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 2">9 out of every 10 suppressed STRs did not become a long-term home</q>. The units went to five places, and the largest is the one rules rarely see: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 5">by far the largest substitution channel</q> was rentals of 30 days or more. Those stays <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 5">are typically furnished, premium-priced corporate/relocation rentals at well above market LTR rates and do little for affordability for ordinary renters</q>. The outcome the bylaws promised is the rarest: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 5">True conversion to long-term rental — the smallest bucket.</q>

Some units did not become any kind of rental at all. <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 5">NYC's vacancy rate did not rise after Local Law 18, suggesting many former STRs did not become any kind of rental</q>. Montreal shows the enforcement problem plainly: as of January 2025, <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 2">more than half of the ~4,000 STR units operating in Montreal were unauthorized</q> despite a provincial registration regime.

Canada has no count to set beside New York's. The researcher whose work is most often cited in support of the Canadian rules conceded the gap himself: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">"It's still unclear what happens to these units after they are removed from the STR listings."</q>

## City rents moved for reasons larger than the rules

Rents did fall in Toronto and Vancouver in 2024 and 2025. In Toronto, <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">November 2024 average apartment/condo rents down 9.4% year-over-year to $2,640</q> was the reported figure. The cause was not the short-term rental file. It was <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">A wave of investor-owned condo completions (a record pipeline from 2021–2022 starts) hitting the rental market as units became unsellable</q>, alongside federal study-permit caps and interest rates squeezing owners into renting what they could not sell. Toronto's decline also arrived with a short-term rental market still in place: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 7">there are still ~9,800 active Airbnb listings (Airbtics, late 2025)</q>, and <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 7">the rent decline did not require the STR market to disappear</q>. Even after those declines, <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">Ontario rents remain 20–25% above pre-COVID levels</q>. In Vancouver, <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 1">CMHC vacancy rates remained near 0.9% for most of 2024</q>, which is not what a city looks like after it has handed thousands of homes to renters.

> **Objection: Toronto's falling rents prove the crackdown worked**
>
> They would only if nothing else had changed, and the construction numbers are on a different scale from the bylaw. In the first half of 2026, <q doc="are-federal-housing-supply-programs-getting-more-homes-built-in-the-greater-toronto-area" section="Section 3">In the City of Toronto, only 156 condominium units were started in the first half of 2026, compared with an average of 7,000 a year over the previous decade</q>. CMHC's reading of the market is that <q doc="are-federal-housing-supply-programs-getting-more-homes-built-in-the-greater-toronto-area" section="Section 3">the decline in condominium starts is not offset by the record high number of rental unit starts.</q> Hamilton, which hoped to win back 650 units, has 2026 year-to-date starts that <q doc="are-federal-housing-supply-programs-getting-more-homes-built-in-the-greater-toronto-area" section="Section 2">are down 39%, at 1,253 against 2,065</q>. The federal housing agency puts the requirement at <q doc="are-federal-housing-supply-programs-getting-more-homes-built-in-the-greater-toronto-area" section="Section 2">roughly 417,000 to 469,000 starts a year to restore 2019 affordability by 2036</q>. Against those figures, a bylaw governing 1,250 listings cannot be the thing that moves the rent index in either direction.

## The clean tests put the rent effect in the low single digits

Jurisdictions that restricted short-term rentals and then measured rents found small effects, and one found the sign reversed. In Los Angeles County, ordinances <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 3">cut listings by ~50% and reduced rents by approximately 2%</q>. Santa Monica, whose rule closely resembles Hamilton's, saw <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§3c">A 60% reduction in Airbnb listings within two years.</q> On rents, the study found <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§3c">No statistically significant effect on residential rents.</q> New York's rents went up: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 3">despite a 90% listings drop, rents rose 3.4% in the first 11 months</q>. Berlin's earlier outright ban <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 3">was quietly partially reversed in 2018 after sustained pushback</q>.

> **Objection: The most-cited study finds Airbnb does raise rents**
>
> It finds a small effect per listing: <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 3">a 10% increase in Airbnb listings raises rents 0.42% and house prices 0.76%</q>, which implies that <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 3">eliminating Airbnb entirely would only reduce rents by single-digit percentages in the highest-exposure neighbourhoods</q>. Removing listings reverses a small push. It does not undo a housing shortage.

> **Objection: Both sides of this argument are paid by someone**
>
> They are, and the reader should hold both. The Canadian figure above comes from <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§3b">a single data briefing, the methodology is not fully disclosed publicly behind its paywall</q>. The research group whose estimates Canadian cities relied on is <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 6">funded in part by the Hotel Association of Canada and the B.C. Hotel Association</q>, and in New York <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 6">the hotel industry spent roughly an order of magnitude more on political contributions than Airbnb in the run-up to Local Law 18</q>. Funding does not settle the numbers. The jurisdictions that ran the policy and then counted the result do, and they land where this article has: listings fall, rents barely move.

## The 28-night cap also closed the month-long stay

The 28-night ceiling did not only end whole-building short lets. It closed the tier that sits between a hotel and a year-long lease, for nurses on contract, people between homes and students on placement. <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§3e">The Hamilton bylaw, by hard-capping any single stay at 28 nights, particularly bites the 30–90 day cohort, even though those stays are widely accepted as the least harmful to long-term housing stock.</q> Nobody measured how many such stays Hamilton had before the bylaw: <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§4">There is no public Hamilton-specific data on the MTR share of its 1,250 units</q>. The same absence runs through the whole Canadian case, which is why the argument never closes: <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§5">No published study, to my knowledge, has tested the specific counterfactual</q> of a city that licensed a furnished tier for stays of a month or more instead of capping nights.

Nuisance and fire safety are a separate question, and they justify the bylaws without any help from the rent argument. <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 8">Safety regulation (post-Old Montreal fire) is plainly justified on its own terms regardless of the housing question.</q> A city can restrict party houses because they ruin streets. It does not need a housing case for that, and it should not borrow one.

## What a city can defend, and what the bylaws promised

A city can defend taking a building back from commercial short lets. The evidence supports that: commercial listings displace rental units, they cluster in a handful of dense blocks, and removing them relieves pressure at the scale of those blocks. Vancouver's returned units and the neighbourhoods named in Montreal, downtown Toronto and West End Vancouver are the shape of a real gain.

What the evidence does not support is the claim the bylaws were argued on, that restricting short-term rentals would lower rents across a city. Where rents fell, construction, migration and interest rates explain the fall, and the fall continued while thousands of short-term listings stayed up. The economist behind the Canadian numbers puts the honest version: regulating short-term rentals <q doc="did-banning-airbnb-actually-fix-canadian-housing-evidence-based-audit" section="Section 8">"can be part of the policy mix, but it's not going to get you much bang for your buck on its own."</q>

Hamilton passed its bylaw during the steepest one-year rent increase any Ontario community tracked that year saw. <q doc="hamiltons-short-term-rental-crackdown-demand-side-disruption-question" section="§2">Hamilton's 14.4% one-year increase from 2022 to 2023 was the largest of any Ontario community tracked by SPRC Hamilton</q>. That is the pattern a city falls into when it reaches for the lever it can pull. The lever was small, and nobody counted what it returned. That is why the argument is still running: the claim a city made was about a rent index, and the effect it bought was a few blocks.

q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Canada's Pharmacare in Practice: Agreements, Coverage, Uptake and Cost Since the 2024 Pharmacare Act
report.body:
## TL;DR

Two years after the *Pharmacare Act* received royal assent on October 10, 2024, the delivered program is confined to four of Canada's 13 provinces and territories — Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon, all signed in February–March 2025 — covering only about 17 per cent of the population, and the federal government has said the agreements are set to end rather than be renewed. What is covered is free contraception and a defined list of diabetes medications (plus menopausal hormone therapy in Manitoba and B.C.), delivered automatically at the pharmacy to anyone eligible for provincial health insurance. Uptake is real but only partially measured: Manitoba reported 139,000 people served in the first 3.5 months, and P.E.I. over 5,000 contraception users and over 20,000 diabetes users, but no national count exists and B.C. and Yukon have published none. The cost of what has actually been delivered is small — $88.1 million in federal contributions in 2025-26 — while the PBO's estimates for a full single-payer program run to an incremental $11.2–13.4 billion a year ($33.2–38.9 billion in total spending, with $1.4–2.2 billion in economy-wide savings), the statutory Committee of Experts priced a more limited essential medicines list at $6–10 billion (net roughly $3 billion), and the Fraser Institute's upper bound without drug-price savings reaches $32.7 billion or more.

## Key Findings

- The *Pharmacare Act* (Bill C-64) received royal assent and came into force October 10, 2024, establishing a framework for universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage of contraception and diabetes medications as a first phase [3].
- Only four jurisdictions have signed agreements: Manitoba (Feb 27, 2025), British Columbia (Mar 6, 2025), Prince Edward Island (Mar 7, 2025) and Yukon (Mar 20, 2025) [1]. No fifth agreement had been signed as of October 2026 [27].
- The four deals cover roughly 17 per cent of the Canadian population [26]; the federal government has indicated the agreements are "set to end in the coming years" rather than be renewed [27].
- The four agreements' commitments total nearly $1 billion over their terms: Manitoba over $219M/4 years [7], B.C. up to $670M/3 years [4], P.E.I. over $30M/4 years [9], Yukon up to $9.5M/4 years [12].
- Coverage is universal within the four jurisdictions — no age, income or private-insurance test — and is delivered at the pharmacy counter, automatically for MSP-enrolled B.C. residents and for auto-enrolled Yukoners [10][4][20].
- The drug lists cover oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, rings, implants and injections [16], plus metformin, insulin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors for diabetes [4]; B.C. and Manitoba add menopause hormone therapy [19][8], and GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic are excluded [8].
- Uptake measured so far: 139,000 Manitobans in the first 3.5 months [25]; over 53,000 Manitobans for birth control in the first year (190,000 prescriptions) [18]; over 5,000 P.E.I. contraception users and over 20,000 P.E.I. diabetes users [21]. B.C. and Yukon have published no user counts.
- Actual federal spending is small: $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [5]; by August 2025 Health Canada had paid $26 million to Manitoba and $3 million to P.E.I. [25].
- The PBO costed the first phase at $1.9 billion over five years, versus the government's $1.5 billion budget figure [6]; about 60 per cent of that $1.5 billion was already spoken for by the four deals by late 2025 [26].
- For a full single-payer program, the PBO estimated an incremental public-sector cost of $11.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28, on total drug spending of $33.2–38.9 billion, with economy-wide savings of $1.4–2.2 billion a year [2].
- The statutory Committee of Experts (November 2025) instead costed an essential medicines list at $6–10 billion a year — net about $3 billion after savings and redirection — and recommended it over bilateral agreements, which it said have drawbacks; the health minister called the report non-binding [24][14].
- The Fraser Institute argues the full-program estimates understate cost because they assume large drug-price cuts and no switching from private plans, putting the no-savings upper bound at $32.7 billion or more [22][15].

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64) actually does and its legislative timeline

The *Pharmacare Act* (Bill C-64, "An Act respecting pharmacare") received royal assent on October 10, 2024 and came into force the same day [3]. It is a framework statute, not a benefit program in itself: it establishes the legal principles for a national universal pharmacare program and directs the federal health minister to pursue bilateral agreements with provinces and territories to deliver the first phase. That first phase is deliberately narrow. Health Canada described it as providing "universal, single-payer, first-dollar access to a range of contraception and diabetes medications" [3], with the government committing to reach agreements that would support "up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada" for free contraception and "the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes" for a suite of diabetes medications [3].

Three operational mandates in the Act were assigned to existing or new institutions rather than to the agreements themselves. The Act requires Canada's Drug Agency to develop "a list of essential drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary, a national bulk purchasing strategy to help further reduce drug prices, and a pan-Canadian strategy on the appropriate use of prescription medications" [3]. Health Canada's own program page confirms that these steps have been completed in some form: the department states it has received advice from Canada's Drug Agency on a national bulk purchasing strategy and a list of essential prescription drugs and related products, and that it has published a pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs and related products [16]. The Act also established a statutory advisory body, the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts, with a mandate to recommend options for the operation and financing of a full national universal single-payer program. The committee was announced on November 14, 2024 and wound up ("sunset") on November 21, 2025 with the tabling of its final report [13].

The legislative timeline is short. The bill was introduced in the House of Commons in February 2024, received royal assent on October 10, 2024, and the bilateral agreement phase began four and a half months later, when Manitoba signed the first deal on February 27, 2025. It is worth noting for accuracy that the committee's terms of reference required its written report by October 10, 2025 — one year after the Act came into force — although the final report was not tabled until November 2025 [13]. Nothing in the Act itself specifies a date by which the broader universal program must exist; it sets the first phase (contraception and diabetes) in motion through agreements and leaves the path to a comprehensive formulary to the committee's recommendations and future government decisions.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed agreements, when, and what the holdouts say

Since the Act came into force, exactly four of Canada's 13 provinces and territories have signed pharmacare funding agreements — three provinces and one territory. Health Canada's own list of bilateral agreements records the sequence precisely: Manitoba on February 27, 2025, British Columbia on March 6, 2025, Prince Edward Island on March 7, 2025, and Yukon on March 20, 2025 [1]. The federal government's summary page is explicit that the total is four: "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free" [1]. No further agreements had been signed as of the late-2026 sources reviewed for this report, although the government publicly committed in the fall of 2025 to pursue more.

**The four agreements and what each bought.** Manitoba's deal was announced as "more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans" [7]. It was the first national pharmacare agreement ever signed. British Columbia's agreement provides up to $670 million in federal funding over three years, and its Plan NP launched March 1, 2026 [4]. Prince Edward Island's agreement is "more than $30 million over four years" [9]. Yukon's is "up to $9.5 million over four years" [12]. Combined, these commitments approach $1 billion over the four-year terms; the Toronto Star put the total at "nearly $1 billion to the four existing agreements, to be doled out over four years" [11].

**Implementation timing.** The four jurisdictions did not all start dispensing at the same time. Manitoba's Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program (MEPP) took effect April 15, 2025 [8]. P.E.I.'s coverage began May 1, 2025 [9][25]. B.C. and Yukon were deliberately later. As of August 2025, CBC reported that two provinces had implemented pharmacare that year while two more jurisdictions were preparing to roll it out — B.C.'s plan was "slated to begin next March," and Yukon's was "on track to start in March 2026" after its agreement had originally indicated a January 2026 start "at the latest" [25]. In the end, B.C.'s Plan NP launched March 1, 2026 [19], and Yukon's program launched April 15, 2026 [20]. The Yukon delay is a minor but real implementation slip, worth noting against the agreements' original timelines [25].

**The holdouts.** Nine jurisdictions had not signed as of mid-2026: Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Quebec, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Nunavut, and the Northwest Territories [25]. This is not because those jurisdictions oppose pharmacare uniformly — every province and territory already runs some form of public drug plan, but coverage, eligibility and cost-sharing vary widely [25]. Several have signalled interest at different times; Nova Scotia said in 2025 it wanted to go "back to the table" on a deal [25]. The dominant story in 2025–2026, however, has been uncertainty at the federal end rather than provincial refusal.

**The 2025–2026 federal stall, then reversal, then stall again.** After the four deals were signed, the Carney government — which took office after the spring 2025 election — signalled repeatedly that expansion was not a priority. In July 2025, Health Minister Marjorie Michel said Canada has "a new government" and is "in a new context" when asked why talks were not progressing, and her office would only commit to "protect" the four existing agreements, not to negotiate more [25]. In September 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney said in Edmonton that his government would strike deals "covering diabetes and birth control drugs and devices with all provinces and territories" — while pointedly declining to commit to expanding the program beyond those two drug classes [11]. But that commitment produced no agreements. By November 2025, Michel confirmed outright that her department is not in active discussions to sign any others, telling CBC: "For now, we have the four provinces with this coverage" [26]. The November 2025 federal budget included no new money for expansion, and the four existing deals covered only "about 17 per cent of the Canadian population" [26].

The Spring 2026 Economic Update then confirmed the stall in fiscal terms: it included no new funding for additional pharmacare deals, which the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives read as an effective abandonment of the national program: "From the Spring Economic Update, it appears that there will be no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals" [5]. CCPA went further, writing that the federal government appears poised to allow existing bilateral funding agreements to expire without renewal [5]. In April 2026, Michel appeared to confirm that reading in the House when pressed on P.E.I.'s funding, saying "These are programs that are set to end in the coming years" [27]. Newfoundland and Labrador's then-health minister Lela Evans said the federal government closed off the negotiations and left Newfoundland Labrador in the cold, describing Ottawa as having "basically closed the door" on N.L. and other provinces [27].

The positions of the nine holdouts are not uniform. As of November 2025, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick said they were ready to talk; Quebec and Alberta said they were waiting to hear back from Ottawa; Alberta also voiced "serious concerns" about the program's long-term sustainability and told Ottawa it wants to decide which medications are covered; and Nova Scotia, which said in mid-2025 it wanted to restart talks, had still not heard back [26][25]. By October 1, 2026, the count was unchanged: only British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon have arrangements, and Newfoundland and Labrador's new health minister, Joedy Wall, had made a federal deal one of his top three priorities while the federal department's only response was that it was "honouring existing pharmacare agreements" [27]. In other words, the reversal in Carney's September 2025 rhetoric never translated into a fifth agreement, and as of the most recent sources the delivered program remains confined to the same four jurisdictions that signed in February–March 2025.

### 3. What is covered: the contraception and diabetes drug lists, eligibility, and how dispensing works

The first phase of national pharmacare covers two therapeutic areas — contraception and diabetes — but the precise product lists are set jurisdiction by jurisdiction within a federal frame, and the four signatories have implemented them with meaningful local differences.

**Eligibility.** The federal program is deliberately universal within a participating jurisdiction. Health Canada's eligibility test has three conditions: you are a resident of a province or territory that has an agreement in place with the federal government, you are eligible for public health insurance in your province or territory, and you have a valid prescription and authorization for a covered medication or related product if needed [10]. There is no age test, no income test, and no means test against private coverage — "You're covered under pharmacare no matter your: age income private or workplace health insurance status" [10]. People covered by federal drug plans (such as Non-Insured Health Benefits, Veterans, RCMP, and the public service plans) retain their existing coverage [10]. In the two largest jurisdictions, access is effectively automatic: in B.C., anyone enrolled in the Medical Services Plan is covered with no separate registration, processed at the pharmacy counter by presenting a prescription and B.C. Services Card [4]; in Yukon, eligible residents are "automatically enrolled" and claims are adjudicated in real time by Pacific Blue Cross, which administers the program, with the program acting as the first payer even for people who also hold private insurance [20].

**Contraception.** Federally, the agreements cover a broad menu — oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, rings, implants and injections [16] — plus the supplies needed to administer and monitor them. This matters for cost because IUDs and implants carry high up-front prices that the pill does not. B.C. is a partial exception on the contraception side only because it had already made prescription contraceptives free before pharmacare — the province was "the first jurisdiction in Canada to provide free prescription birth control" — so its Plan NP mainly adds the diabetes and menopause-hormone lists, while existing contraceptive coverage continues under the plan [19][4]. Manitoba's MEPP folded the earlier provincial free-birth-control program into a broader no-cost list [8]. P.E.I. covers "most contraceptives" [25]. All four signatories cover contraception at no cost at the point of dispensing, though the federal pages are careful that only "listed" products are free [17].

**Diabetes medications.** The federal frame lists the drug classes: metformin; insulin; sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors; and the agreements also improve access to diabetes devices and supplies (blood glucose monitors and test strips, and newer insulin pump technologies) [16][20]. B.C.'s published Plan NP list is the most granular public example: covered drugs include "insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, such as glyburide and gliclazide, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, saxagliptin, linagliptin and pioglitazone" [4]. Three of those — saxagliptin, linagliptin and pioglitazone — require a prescriber's Special Authority request in B.C., while the others are covered at 100 per cent without one [19]. Manitoba's MEPP covers most diabetes medications at no cost with no deductible, but explicitly excludes Ozempic (semaglutide), because "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories" [8]. That exclusion is a useful marker of the program's limits: the first phase covers the older, cheaper diabetes drugs, not the newer GLP-1 class, which was not on the federal discussion list.

**Menopause hormone therapy.** Two jurisdictions went beyond the federal two-area frame using the federal money and provincial funds. Manitoba's MEPP includes hormone replacement therapy at no cost, and B.C.'s Plan NP covers a defined list of menopause hormone therapies at 100 per cent: oral conjugated estrogen, oral medroxyprogesterone, oral micronized progesterone, vaginal estrogen, topical estrogen and estrogen/progesterone gels and patches, and oral estradiol [8][19]. B.C. estimated roughly 160,000 residents with menopausal symptoms would benefit [4]. Yukon and P.E.I.'s programs are described as contraception and diabetes only.

**What pharmacare does not cover.** The federal guidance is explicit that the program only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee, and does not cover delivery fees or pharmacist prescribing fees [17]. It also does not cover drugs outside the two lists, devices beyond what the agreements specify, or anything dispensed in a non-participating jurisdiction.

**Scale of what is at stake.** Health Canada frames the phase-one economics with two sets of numbers. About "3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes"; 2018 diabetes-related health-system costs were estimated at "$27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028" [16]. On drug prices, the department cites typical annual costs before coverage of roughly "$100 per year" for metformin, "$900 and $1,700 per year" for insulin, and "$100 to over $1,000 per year" for sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors [16]. B.C. adds the patient-side figures from Diabetes Canada: up to $18,300 per year for Type 1 diabetes and up to $10,000 per year for Type 2 diabetes, and notes that uninsured menopause hormone therapy runs $240 to $1,800 per year [4].

**A delivery wrinkle worth recording.** Because the federal program is first payer in several jurisdictions, some private insurers have begun delisting the drugs Ottawa now covers — a point raised by pharmacists in both P.E.I. and Manitoba. The consequence is not usually a loss of coverage (the public plan picks the drug up), but it can create edge cases, such as a P.E.I. university student studying out of province who must return to a P.E.I. pharmacy to fill a drug their parents' insurer has dropped [25]. Pharmacists also reported having to adjust billing systems for only the federally eligible medications, which broke the seamlessness of high-volume dispensing [25]. These are implementation frictions, not failures, but they are part of what has actually been delivered.

### 4. How many people are using it: uptake, claims and dispensing data

There is no single national count of pharmacare users, because the program is delivered through four separate provincial and territorial systems and no central agency publishes consolidated claims data. What exists is jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction reporting, of uneven recency and detail. The available numbers are nonetheless substantial relative to the populations involved, and they show the program reaching more people than the bare "eligible" denominators alone would suggest.

**Manitoba — the most complete uptake data.** Manitoba has published the most granular figures. In the first three and a half months of federal pharmacare operating there (from April 15, 2025), the province said the program "has supported 139,000 people" [25]. That figure spans contraception, diabetes, and the provincially added HRT and HIV-prevention (PrEP/PEP) categories. On the contraception side specifically, the province reported a full-year count: "Between Oct. 2, 2024, and Oct. 21, 2025, more than 53,000 people got free birth control through the program," with 190,000 prescriptions dispensed across all types of contraceptives over that period, nearly nine in 10 of them for oral birth control [18]. Note the date range begins before MEPP launched, because Manitoba had already introduced a provincial free-birth-control program in October 2024, which MEPP then absorbed [18]. The 139,000 figure in the first 3.5 months is the closest thing to a single program-wide uptake number for any jurisdiction and implies a pace well beyond the 53,000 who used the narrower provincial contraception program over a full year.

**Prince Edward Island.** P.E.I.'s figures come from the province's own three-year Pharmacy Plus anniversary release. "Since launching on May 1, 2025, over 5,000 Islanders have accessed free contraception, saving more than $500,000 in out-of-pocket costs, while over 20,000 people with diabetes have benefited from covered medications and supplies, saving more than $200,000 in out-of-pocket costs" [21]. Those are people counts, not prescription counts, and they were reported in late October 2025, about six months into the program. Against P.E.I.'s small population, more than 20,000 diabetes-medication users is a large share — consistent with the province's own expectation that the deal would support "over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes" [9], which the early count already exceeded.

**British Columbia.** B.C.'s Plan NP launched only on March 1, 2026, so there is little dispensing data yet. The province's planning numbers are the best available proxy: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [4]. These are eligibility-scale estimates, not recorded users, and should be read as the ceiling rather than the observed count. The province reports coverage is automatic for MSP enrollees, so actual uptake will depend on prescribing and dispensing behaviour, which no public source yet measures [4].

**Yukon.** Yukon's program launched April 15, 2026 — the most recent start — and, as a Yukon News report put it, "data specific to the Yukon is not available" as of launch [20]. The territory's agreement-scale figures are "more than 12,000 Yukoners" for contraception and "over 3,000 residents with diabetes" [12]. A news report's headline described "Some 15K Yukoners" as newly able to access low-cost prescriptions at launch [20]. No claims or user counts have yet been published.

**What the uptake data can and cannot show.** Three points follow from these figures. First, in the two jurisdictions with real dispensing counts — Manitoba and P.E.I. — uptake ran ahead of or in line with the governments' own eligible-population projections, suggesting the "automatic, no-deductible" design is being used. Second, the Manitoba numbers show the dominance of the pill within contraception use (nine of ten prescriptions), while the device and long-acting reversible methods (IUDs, implants) that the program explicitly covers are a minority of the recorded volume — an observation the data supports but does not explain. Third, there is a genuine measurement gap: B.C., the largest signatory by population, has not yet published user counts, and no jurisdiction publishes a consolidated national figure, so any statement that "X Canadians are using pharmacare" would be an inference assembled from four different provincial datasets on four different timelines rather than a reported statistic. The honest current estimate — my own arithmetic assembled from the sources above, not a published statistic — adding Manitoba's 139,000 (mid-2025, partial-year) and P.E.I.'s reported users (over 5,000 for contraception and over 20,000 for diabetes, late 2025), then the as-yet-uncounted B.C. and Yukon populations, is that the number of people who have actually filled a pharmacare-covered prescription runs into the low hundreds of thousands — while the eligible population across the four signatories is in the order of a million or more once B.C.'s 570,000-person diabetes cohort is included. That is an inference from the sources above, not a figure any government has published.

### 5. What the program costs now and what the PBO and other independent estimates say the full program would cost

Cost figures for pharmacare divide into three distinct layers that are often conflated: what the first phase actually costs now, what the *Pharmacare Act*'s first phase was estimated to cost over five years, and what a full universal single-payer program would cost. The Parliamentary Budget Officer has produced estimates for the latter two; other independent analysts (the Fraser Institute, the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts, and earlier advisory work) have produced competing numbers for the full program, and they differ for identifiable methodological reasons.

**What is being spent now.** The first phase is small relative to both the rhetoric and the full-program figures. The federal contribution to the four signatory jurisdictions was "$88.1 million" in 2025-26 and is projected to rise to "$269.6 million by 2028-29" [5]. Through the first months of the program, actual disbursements were modest: by August 2025, "Health Canada has paid $26 million to Manitoba and $3 million to P.E.I. to cover these medications" [25]. Those numbers reflect a program that had been operating for only a few months in two small provinces; they are not annualized totals. The four agreements' headline commitments are larger over their full terms — Manitoba "more than $219 million over four years" [7], B.C. "up to $670 million ... over three years" [4], P.E.I. "more than $30 million over four years" [9], Yukon "up to $9.5 million over four years" [12] — but even summed, they are under $1 billion spread over the agreement terms [11], a fraction of what a full program would cost.

**The first-phase legislative estimate.** When Bill C-64 was before Parliament, the PBO costed the bill itself. Its legislative costing found the first phase "will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years" [6]. The government's own budget had pegged the first phase at $1.5 billion over five years, so the PBO's number was roughly $400 million higher — the gap the Fraser Institute highlighted in arguing that the federal government's estimates don't reflect the true costs of the program [15][6]. Two modelling choices in the PBO's first-phase estimate matter. The PBO assumed the new program would cover 100 per cent of costs for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons, plus the uncovered portions for people who do have plans — and it explicitly did not model the behavioural effect of people with existing private insurance switching into the public plan [6]. The Fraser Institute's critique turns exactly on that omission: because 81 per cent of Canadians had some drug insurance in 2019, the estimates that assume nobody already covered will switch to the new national plan understate what a genuinely universal first-dollar program costs if it becomes the first payer [15].

**The full single-payer program: the PBO's two numbers.** The PBO's standalone October 2023 report — *Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan*, prepared before the Act but still the reference estimate for the full program — models a universal single-payer plan over five years starting January 1, 2024. Its headline figures: the incremental cost to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28 [2]. Total drug expenditures under the plan would be $33.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $38.9 billion in 2027-28 [2]. Critically, the PBO also estimated economy-wide savings: cost savings on drug expenditures of $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28 [2]. In other words, the PBO's full plan costs governments an incremental $11–13 billion a year but reduces total national drug spending by $1.4–2.2 billion a year, because single-payer purchasing and formulary discipline cut prices enough to offset much of the public cost. Those savings are the mechanism everyone else's estimates turn on.

**The competing independent estimates.** Three other sets of numbers sit alongside the PBO's, and they disagree for identifiable reasons.

The **Hoskins Report** (the 2019 Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare) produced the other frequently cited figure; the Fraser Institute summarizes the pair as a fully universal single-payer pharmacare program that could cost between $13.4 billion and $15.3 billion in 2027/28 [22]. The $13.4 billion is the PBO's 2027-28 incremental cost; $15.3 billion is the Hoskins figure for the same year.

The **Fraser Institute** argues both are too low. Its commentators cite economist Jack Mintz: the PBO and Hoskins numbers assume an immediate and significant reduction in negotiated drug prices, which is unlikely to occur, so the actual annual cost could be much higher at $32.7 billion or beyond [22]. That $32.7 billion is not a full independent costing but a sensitivity: it is what the program costs if the assumed price reductions do not materialize and the public plan instead absorbs existing spending levels. The Fraser Institute also stresses a distributional point: a single-payer plan "would simply shift the cost from private and/or provincial plans to the federal government for the majority of Canadians already insured" [22] — a large fiscal transfer even if the national drug bill falls.

The **National Pharmacare Committee of Experts** (the Act's own statutory committee) published the most recent independent estimate, in its November 2025 final report. It frames the question differently from the PBO: it costs a federal essential medicines list — the "fill the gaps for everyone" version — rather than absorbing all drug spending. Its conclusion: "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars" [24], with the chair, Dr. Navindra Persaud, telling reporters the additional net cost to government would be "around $3 billion a year" once existing spending is redirected and bulk-purchasing savings are counted [14]. The committee's accompanying status-quo-versus-pharmacare table (its own estimates using IQVIA, CIHI and PBO data) shows why: under the status quo it projects roughly $9.5 billion out-of-pocket, $17.3 billion private insurance and $18.8 billion public in 2025; under its pharmacare model those fall to $6.8 billion, $12.5 billion and $13.6 billion respectively, with a new $8 billion federal pharmacare line [24]. The committee also records that total prescribed-drug spending in Canada rose from "$34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024" — a $10 billion increase in five years — which is the baseline a full program would be reorganizing [24].

**Reconciling the disagreement.** The spread — $6–10 billion (committee) versus $11.2–13.4 billion incremental (PBO) versus up to $32.7 billion (Fraser/Mintz) — is mostly about scope and assumptions, not about anyone's arithmetic being wrong. The committee is costing a narrower thing (an essential medicines list, first-dollar, with existing public and private plans continuing for everything else); the PBO is costing a broader thing (a full single-payer plan absorbing all prescription drug spending, with large assumed price reductions); and the Mintz figure is the PBO scope without the price reductions. A careful reader should therefore treat $13.4 billion a year as the PBO's central estimate for a comprehensive single-payer plan *with* savings assumptions, up to $32.7 billion as the no-savings upper bound, and $6–10 billion (net roughly $3 billion) as the committee's estimate for the more limited essential-medicines first step it actually recommended. The government itself, when it announced the contraception-and-diabetes first phase in February 2024, cited a far smaller "$1 billion annually" for just those two drug classes [22].

**What this means for the delivered program.** The gap between the estimates and the reality on the ground is the single most important fact in this area. The first phase that has actually been delivered costs the federal government under $100 million a year so far [5], and even at its projected 2028-29 peak it is $269.6 million [5] — about 2 per cent of the PBO's estimated incremental cost of a full single-payer program, and about one-quarter of the government's own $1 billion-a-year announcement figure for the two drug classes. The reason is that only four of 13 jurisdictions have signed, only two had substantial operating time in 2025, and the first phase covers a deliberately limited formulary. Most of what "pharmacare" would cost — on any estimate — has not yet been committed, and the Spring 2026 Economic Update's decision to add no new funding [5], followed by Carney's commitment to more deals [11], leaves the question of whether the rest of it will ever be spent unresolved.


## Open questions

**Actual national uptake remains unmeasured.** No government publishes a consolidated count of how many Canadians have filled a pharmacare-covered prescription. Manitoba and P.E.I. have released partial counts on their own timelines; B.C. and Yukon have released none since their March and April 2026 launches. The single most useful missing number is a claims-level total — people and prescriptions, by drug class — across all four jurisdictions, which would let anyone verify whether the "eligible" denominators (570,000 in B.C. alone) are actually turning into filled prescriptions.

**The future of the four existing agreements is unresolved.** The federal government has not said whether it will renew the four bilateral agreements when they expire (CCPA and the federal health minister's April 2026 statement both point to expiry rather than renewal, but no formal decision has been announced). Whether the 17 per cent of Canadians now covered keep their coverage past the agreement end-dates is an open question with no published answer.

**Whether a fifth agreement will ever be signed.** Carney publicly committed in September 2025 to sign deals with the remaining provinces and territories, and several provinces (Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador) have said they want one. No agreement has been signed since Yukon's in March 2025. What, if anything, has blocked a fifth deal — funding, the drug list, or the federal government's own priorities — has not been authoritatively explained.

**The cost of a full program beyond the PBO's 2023 model.** The PBO has not re-costed a full single-payer program since the Act passed; its $11.2–13.4 billion incremental figure is a 2023 model of a hypothetical plan, not a costing of what the Act will actually produce. No independent body has published an updated full-program costing since the Committee of Experts' November 2025 report, and the committee itself costed only an essential medicines list, not a comprehensive formulary.

**Coverage was thin on two points.** First, no public source publishes the complete federal "common list" of contraception and diabetes drugs used in the negotiations; the report above reconstructs coverage from B.C.'s and Manitoba's published lists, which are the best available but not necessarily identical to what the other two jurisdictions list. Second, the delivered program's actual fiscal cost in 2025-26 was available only through CCPA's reading of the budget documents and CBC's partial disbursement figures; Health Canada's own accounting of what it has actually paid each jurisdiction was not found.

## Beyond this question

The pharmacare story is a clean case study in how a statutory framework and a delivered program can diverge. The *Pharmacare Act* passed with universalist language — "universal, single-payer, first-dollar" — but its operative mechanism is bilateral negotiation, and after two years that mechanism has produced coverage for four of thirteen jurisdictions and roughly 17 per cent of the population, with the federal government itself saying the agreements will end. Anyone tracking whether Canadian social-policy legislation "works" should measure what the bilateral agreements actually delivered, not what the Act's preamble promises: here the two have moved in opposite directions. The same pattern — a national statute, a first phase funded through discretionary bilateral deals, and a government later declining to extend the deals — is worth watching in the parallel rollout of dental care, where the same confidence-and-supply political logic applied.

The cost debate also carries a lesson that generalizes beyond pharmacare. The widely cited "$13.4 billion" and "$32.7 billion" figures are not two measurements of the same program but two different scopes and two different assumptions about drug-price savings. In any future reporting or policy work on pharmacare, the responsible practice is to state which program is being costed (essential medicines list versus full single-payer) and whether the estimate assumes negotiated price reductions, because those two choices move the answer by a factor of three.
