## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone bans or restrictions, and what exactly do the policies require?

The cleanest global count comes from UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring (GEM) team, which maintains country profiles of phone policies. As of its March 2026 update, it counted **114 education systems with a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide** — and the expansion has been rapid: fewer than 1 in 4 countries (24%) had bans when the policy was first monitored for the 2023 GEM Report, that rose to 40% by early 2025, and to 58% by March 2026 [3]. The GEM team's own framing is that bans are spreading worldwide as the policy debate rages on. These counts treat a "ban" loosely — they cover systems that restrict use to varying degrees and for varying ages, not only total prohibitions — so the headline number is a measure of policy spread, not of policy strength.

**Ontario.** Ontario's restriction is provincial, not national, and is set out in the provincial Code of Conduct through a ministry policy (PPM 128) effective 1 September 2024. The government's own page states the operative rule plainly: students in Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobile devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher, while students in Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher [6]. Devices must be kept on silent and out of view, and social media is removed from school networks and devices. In other words, Ontario's policy is a class-time restriction for older students and a full-school-day restriction for younger ones, with teacher discretion retained. Unlike France or the Australian states, it is implemented through a provincial policy directive rather than a statute, and enforcement detail is left to boards and schools.

**England.** England is a non-statutory example, and one of the most studied. UNESCO's monitoring describes it as issuing strengthened guidance encouraging schools to prohibit mobile phones during the school day, with the expectation reinforced through school inspection frameworks, yet leaving implementation decisions to individual schools [3]. The Department for Education issued guidance in February 2024 telling schools to prohibit phone use throughout the school day, but it is not a legal requirement; schools choose their own approach, which is why English studies (below) compare "restrictive" against "permissive" schools rather than banned against unbanned ones.

**The Netherlands.** The Dutch measure is likewise a government-promoted agreement rather than a law. It was first introduced in January 2024 for secondary education and extended to include primary education from the 2024/2025 school year, with the stated aim of encouraging discussion and social interaction and addressing cyberbullying [8]. Eurydice notes the measure is government-promoted but "it is up to the individual education institutions to provide concrete rules and to determine what the policy will look like in practice" [8]. Coverage is broad — surveys found nearly all secondary schools complied — but the binding force is an agreement between schools and the ministry, not legislation.

**Australian states.** Australia's bans are state-by-state and mostly statutory or policy-based, and they now cover effectively the whole country's public schools. The Guardian's timeline: "Victoria moved early, banning phones in public primary and secondary schools in 2020. By term four, 2023, Western Australia Tasmania, New South Wales and South Australia had followed suit; Queensland restricted phones in term one, 2024" [10]. The policies differ in detail — Victoria requires phones switched off and securely stored all day; New South Wales bans use from the start to the end of the school day; Queensland requires "away for the day" — but the common design is a full-school-day ban in public schools, often extended to non-government schools later.

**Other notable jurisdictions.** France was among the earliest and most cited national bans: a 2018 law prohibited phone use for students in primary and lower secondary schools throughout the school day, a policy the Swedish replication paper references as the model others copied. Spain has no single national law; instead autonomous regions enacted bans from 2015 onward, and two regions (Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha) are the basis of the most-cited Spanish evaluation. In the United States there is no federal ban; UNESCO's count shows 39 states with statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring districts to adopt restricting policies (24) [3]. The US pouch study adds that "as of 2026, roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide have enacted legislation limiting student phone access" [14]. Norway — the source of the most-cited quasi-experiment — has no national ban; individual municipalities and middle schools chose to ban, which is exactly what allowed Abrahamsson to compare schools that banned against those that did not.

Three structural facts matter for interpreting every evaluation that follows. First, "ban" means very different things across these jurisdictions — a class-time restriction (Ontario's older grades), a full-school-day physical separation (Victoria, Yondr pouches), a teacher-discretion rule, or a ministry-encouraged agreement (England, the Netherlands). Second, most of the highest-profile bans are too recent to have mature evaluation data: Ontario's 2024 policy, the Dutch 2024 measure, England's 2024 guidance, and the Australian state bans from 2020–2024 have only a few years of post-implementation observation, and several have no rigorous outcome evaluation at all yet. Third, the strongest causal studies come disproportionately from places where the policy was *not* nationally uniform — England before 2024, Norway, Sweden, Spain's two regions, Florida's district, Rio de Janeiro — because variation across schools or regions is what makes a credible counterfactual possible.

### 2. What have evaluations measured about learning and academic outcomes, and what do they find?

The learning evidence splits sharply by study design and country, and the headline numbers range from substantial gains to precisely estimated zero.

**England (Beland & Murphy, 2016).** The foundational causal study used the staggered introduction of phone bans in English secondary schools between 2001 and 2011, linked to administrative GCSE records. It found that student performance in high-stakes exams significantly increased post-ban, by about 0.07 standard deviations on average, and that the increases were driven by the lowest-achieving students [5]. The effect was concentrated in the lowest quartile of prior achievement, with no significant effect for high achievers. This is a difference-in-differences design on real exam data, but it rests on a school survey with a 21% response rate — a weakness the authors themselves had to confront, and the central reason a replication was run.

**Sweden (Kessel, Hardardottir & Tyrefors, 2020).** The replication, using Swedish data and the same empirical design but a ~75% survey response rate and the universe of grade-9 schools, found the opposite. The authors state that in Sweden they find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains [12]. Their point estimates were never significantly different from zero, and in the most controlled specification they "can reject positive effect sizes larger than 1 percent of a standard deviation" [12]. They offer two candidate explanations for the divergence from England: Sweden is the most computer-dense country in Europe (with separate laptops already ubiquitous in classrooms, so the phone was not the only screen), and teacher-level phone bans may already have been in place in practice regardless of formal school policy. The contrast matters: it is the cleanest demonstration that a finding from one country does not automatically transfer.

**Spain (Beneito & Vicente-Chirivella, 2022).** Using the 2015 regional bans in Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha and a synthetic-control approach against the other Spanish regions, this study found large PISA effects for Galicia: students' PISA scores in Galicia improved by around 10 points in maths and 12 points in sciences relative to a synthetic Galicia, equivalent by the authors' (Woessmann-derived) conversion to "0.6–0.8 years of learning in maths and around 0.72 to near one year of learning in sciences" [9]. Those are among the largest claimed effects in the whole literature, and they come from a regional-level design with only two treated regions — the study itself notes incomplete data from Castilla-La Mancha affected comparability, and a two-region synthetic control is necessarily fragile.

**Florida (Figlio & Ozek, 2025).** The first large US statewide evaluation used a 2023 Florida law requiring phones to be off and out of sight all day in a large urban district. Comparing schools with high versus low pre-ban phone activity, it found test scores improved by 0.6 percentiles, with the ban increasing spring test scores 1.1 percentiles in the second year, larger for male students (1.4 percentiles) and middle/high schools (1.3 percentiles) [1]. It also found the ban significantly improved student attendance, especially for unexcused absences, by roughly 5–10% of the comparison-group mean — and the authors estimate that attendance improvement "may explain a large fraction" of the test-score gains, a mechanism the Indian trial (below) explicitly did not find.

**United States, national pouch study (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow & Jacob, NBER WP 35132, 2026).** The largest and most rigorous study to date evaluated Yondr lockable pouches across the country — 4,608 adopting schools — using a pre-registered, staggered difference-in-differences design with matched comparison schools. Its academic-achievement finding is a precise null in the aggregate: average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero, with the authors able to rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations over three years [14]. Beneath that average is a statistically significant but small positive effect for high-school mathematics — roughly 0.024 student-level standard deviations, which the authors equate to about 0.9 percentile points — while middle schools show small negative effects [14]. The Stanford summary of the same study put it in plain terms: almost zero difference in test scores on average, with a slight bump in high-school mathematics but a slight decrease in middle-school test scores [13].

**England, SMART Schools (Goodyear et al., 2025).** The largest direct observational study of the post-2024 English guidance era, covering 1,227 adolescents in 30 schools, found no attainment difference between restrictive and permissive schools: no significant differences in pupil outcomes between permissive and restrictive schools for attainment in English (adjusted odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 0.85–2.47, p = 0.18) or Maths (adjusted odds ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.45–2.27, p = 0.98) [2]. This is a cross-sectional comparison, not a causal estimate, and attainment was teacher-reported, but it directly tests the policy as England actually implemented it — guidance, not law — and finds nothing.

**India, the randomized trial (Sungu, Choudhury & Bjerre-Nielsen, Science, 2026).** The only true randomized controlled trial in this literature assigned 16,683 students across 10 higher-education institutions in Odisha to mandatory in-class phone collection or a control condition for a semester. It improved academic performance, particularly among lower-performing students and first-year undergraduates, with effects minimal among higher-performing, postgraduate, and STEM students, and it reduced disparities in GPA [11]. Crucially, "attendance rates did not change," so the authors attribute the gains to attention and classroom dynamics rather than more time in class [11]. This is tertiary education in a specific Indian context, so it is not directly a school-phone-ban result — but it is the cleanest causal test of the underlying mechanism (removing the device from the room) and it finds the mechanism real, concentrated on lower performers.

**Reconciling the spread.** The strongest reading across all of this is not "bans work" or "bans do nothing," but that the effect of a ban on *measured* learning depends on who is being studied, what they would otherwise be doing, and how well the policy actually removes the phone. The two null results in rich, device-saturated school systems (Sweden; the US national average) sit alongside positive results in England (2011-era, pre-smartphone-saturation data), Spain (two regions), Florida (second-year effects), and an Indian RCT (the device physically removed from the room). The effects that do appear are concentrated in the lowest-performing students, in mathematics, and in secondary rather than middle school — and several of the strongest effects travel partly through attendance, not through in-class attention alone. No study yet shows large, uniform gains across an entire school system from a national ban.

### 3. What have evaluations measured about attention, distraction and phone use behaviour?

Attention and distraction are the outcomes bans are *most* often justified by, but they are among the *least* well measured by the strongest studies — because attention is usually self- or teacher-reported rather than administratively recorded. The evidence falls into two tiers: hard measurement of phone use (which shows bans do what they say), and softer reports of attention and behaviour (which mostly agree among teachers but show little in student self-reports).

**Bans reduce in-school phone use — the first-stage is real.** Every study that measured phone use directly found the policy changed it. In Florida, smartphone activity "dropping to about one-third of the pre-ban levels in the first two months of the ban" [1]. In the US national pouch study, the teacher-reported share of students using phones in class for personal reasons fell from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent), a substantially larger decline than in non-adopting schools, and GPS ping data confirmed a large, persistent decline [14]. In the English SMART Schools study, restrictive-school students had lower in-school phone time (−0.67 h) and social media time (−0.54 h) than permissive-school students — but "there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [2]. That last point is the central caveat for attention claims: the ban compresses use at school but does not reduce the total day's use, because students compensate outside school hours.

**Teacher and principal reports of improved attention are strong but are perception data.** The Australian state evaluations are essentially all of this kind. In New South Wales, a survey of almost 1,000 principals one year in found 95% of principals still supported the ban, 81% said it had improved students' learning, 86% said it had improved socialisation, and 87% believed students were less distracted in the classroom [10]. In South Australia, 70% of teachers reported increased focus and engagement during learning time, and 64% reported a lower frequency of critical incidents at school as a result of device use [10]. The Dutch government-commissioned survey of 317 secondary school leaders, 313 primary schools and 12 focus groups found "children found it easier to concentrate (75%), the social environment was better (59%) and some said results had improved (28%)" [7]. In the Indian RCT, classroom observation — an independent, non-self-reported measure — "found less disruptive behavior and fewer off-topic conversations, along with greater teacher engagement" [11].

**But student self-reports and the null studies point the other way.** The US national pouch study, which had student survey data on classroom attention, found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [14]. The authors explicitly flag that differential pre-trends limit the conclusions for attention, but the honest summary is that the most rigorous US study did not find the attention gain that teachers in Australia report. The English SMART Schools study likewise found no difference in teacher-reported disruptive classroom behaviour between restrictive and permissive schools [2].

**Reconciling these.** The two findings are not as contradictory as they look, for three reasons. First, teachers and principals observe a real change in *device use* and report it as improved focus; the US study confirms the device-use change is real and large. Second, student self-report of "attention" may be a poor instrument — students may not perceive their own distraction, or the question may not map onto what the ban changed. Third, the outcomes that matter most for the justification — test scores — are measured precisely in the US study and barely move, which suggests that the perceived attention gain either does not translate into learning, or that phones were displacing a different distraction (peers, off-task talk) rather than a uniquely damaging one. The Florida and US studies both found that the transition itself creates *more* disruption at first (see section 6), which is consistent with students substituting toward other off-task behaviour when the device is removed.

The strongest single causal claim about attention in the whole literature is the Indian RCT: phones physically removed from the room produced measurable learning gains with attendance held constant, which the authors read as evidence the mechanism ran through attention and classroom dynamics rather than through attendance [11]. That is an inference from the design, not a direct measure of attention — but it is the cleanest demonstration that removing the device can matter in a room where students have no other screens.

### 4. What have evaluations measured about bullying and cyberbullying?

Bullying is where the evidence for bans is most consistently positive — and where the measurement is most contested, because "bullying" is counted in very different ways across studies.

**Spain.** The Spanish regional study found that after the 2015 bans in Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha, "bullying incidence fell by around 9.5% to 18% over its pre-intervention levels among teenagers in the treated regions" [9]. This is a difference-in-differences/synthetic-control design using administrative bullying reports, and it is the study's second headline result alongside the PISA gains.

**Norway.** The Abrahamsson working paper and its published version find post-ban bullying declines for both genders, an effect that persists across both "strict" (phones handed in) and "lenient" (phones allowed at breaks, silent in class) policies. The working-paper magnitude quoted in commentary is "0.42 of an SD for girls, 0.39 of an SD for boys" [18] — a large effect — and the peer-reviewed abstract states simply that bans "lower bullying for both genders" [4]. The second Marginal Revolution post quotes the paper directly: for bullying there is not much difference dependent on the type of policy implemented, neither for girls nor for boys — meaning the mere existence of a restrictive policy, not its strictness, was what mattered [18].

**United States.** Here the picture is more cautious. The pre-registered national pouch study found "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying" — and flagged differential pre-trends as a limit on what can be concluded [14]. The Stanford summary rendered this as "not even on perceived cyberbullying" [13]. Note the qualifier: the US measure is *perceived online* bullying, a single survey item, whereas the Spanish and Norwegian measures are broader school-bullying incidence or administrative counts. So the US null is not directly comparable to the European positives, and the study itself warns against strong conclusions on that outcome.

**Australia and the Netherlands.** The Australian evaluations report reductions in "critical incidents" involving devices rather than measured bullying rates — South Australia's teachers reported 64% fewer critical incidents related to device use [10], and Victoria's independent evaluation similarly reported fewer critical incidents involving phones. The Dutch rationale named cyberbullying explicitly as a motivation, but the Dutch survey did not measure bullying outcomes.

**How to read it.** Across the studies that measured bullying directly — Spain and Norway — the finding is consistently a reduction, and the Norwegian effect is large. The one high-quality study that measured a cyberbullying-flavoured outcome and found nothing (the US pouch study) used the weakest and narrowest bullying measure (a single self-report item about *perceived online* bullying) and was unable to cleanly identify that effect. The Böttger & Zierer meta-analysis, pooling the early studies, found the social well-being domain — dominated by bullying measures — was where bans had their significant effect: d = 0.22, p < 0.001, against a non-significant d = 0.05 for performance [16]. The most defensible statement is that there is reasonably consistent quasi-experimental evidence that school phone restrictions reduce bullying, and that the magnitude ranges from modest (Spain, ~10–18%) to large (Norway, ~0.4 SD), while the only rigorous test of the narrower outcome "perceived online bullying" found nothing. No study yet measures whether bans reduce the *total* volume of online harassment, since most online bullying happens outside school hours — the same compensation problem that limits the mental-health and total-use findings.

### 5. What have evaluations measured about mental health and wellbeing?

Mental health is the outcome where the strongest causal evidence most directly contradicts the public rationale for bans — and where the studies' own nuance is most frequently lost in summaries.

**England (SMART Schools, 2025).** The only study designed specifically to test the mental-health claim, using a nationally representative sample of 1,227 adolescents across 30 schools and the validated WEMWBS scale, found nothing: mean mental-wellbeing score was 47 (SD 9), with an adjusted mean difference of −0.48 between restrictive and permissive schools (95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62) [2]. There were also no differences in anxiety, depression, sleep duration or efficiency, physical activity, problematic social media use, or motives for use. The authors' interpretation is blunt: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents," and the findings "do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form" [2]. The mechanism they identify is the compensation problem already noted: restrictive schools cut in-school phone time by 0.67 hours and social media time by 0.54 hours, but "there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [2] — students simply made the time up, so total exposure did not fall.

**Norway (Abrahamsson).** The Norwegian study is the one most cited *for* mental-health benefits, and the honest reading is more limited than the headlines. The peer-reviewed abstract states that banning smartphones "has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences," and that bans "reduce psychological health care use among girls" [4]. The working-paper detail, relayed in Marginal Revolution's close reading, shows what that means: girls' visits to GPs for psychological symptoms fell by 0.22 on average and specialist-care visits fell by 2–3 per year, while the paper itself found "no effect on students' likelihood (extensive margin) of being diagnosed or treated by specialists or GPs for a psychological symptom and diseases" [18]. In other words, girls consulted less, but there was no change in whether they were diagnosed or treated — a reduction in help-seeking contact, not a demonstrated improvement in mental health. The grade effects and the visit effects were also not correlated in the data, so the mental-health change does not explain the grade change.

**United States (pouch study).** The pre-registered national study found a *negative* short-run wellbeing effect and only a later recovery: student-reported subjective wellbeing "declines in the year of adoption and then rebounds, becoming positive by the second post-adoption year. The decline is roughly 0.2 student-level standard deviations, followed by an increase of 0.16 standard deviations" [14]. The authors read this as short-term disruption followed by adaptation, and they are explicit that it is suggestive rather than conclusive given the short panel. The Stanford summary's plain-language version: disciplinary issues dissipated after the first year, and "in the third year, student well-being was higher than before the phones were stashed away" [13]. So the best US evidence suggests the *transition* temporarily hurts wellbeing before any benefit appears — not that bans are a straightforward mental-health win.

**What the disagreement means.** These are not contradictory findings so much as findings about different things. England measured *self-reported mental wellbeing and symptoms* in a cross-section of schools and found no difference. Norway measured *health-care utilisation* (visits) using administrative records in an event-study design and found a reduction for girls, but no change in diagnosis or treatment. The US measured *subjective wellbeing* longitudinally and found a dip then a recovery. The most careful synthesis is: there is no credible evidence that school phone bans improve adolescent mental health or reduce symptoms; there is some evidence that bans reduce girls' psychological help-seeking contact in Norway; and there is some evidence that the immediate transition period reduces subjective wellbeing before recovering. The claim that bans improve mental health — the claim most often attached to the Norwegian study in advocacy — is not supported by the study itself, which reports no average effect.

A final point on direction of inference. The strongest causal evidence on *screens and wellbeing* (outside the school-ban literature) is the environment-scale work — Facebook's college rollout worsened mental health, deactivation improved it, broadband rollout raised diagnosed mental disorders — but those concern total platform exposure, which a school-day ban barely touches. A ban that shifts an hour of use from the school day to the evening does not reduce total exposure, which is precisely what SMART Schools measured. That is why the school-ban literature, on its own terms, has so little to say about mental health.

### 6. How strong is the evidence overall, and where do the sources disagree?

The overall strength of the evidence is modest, improving fast, and sharply uneven across outcomes. The best way to see this is to separate what is well established from what is contested.

**What is well established.** (1) Bans reduce in-school phone use, substantially and measurably — Florida's one-third reduction [1], the US pouch study's 61%→13% teacher-reported drop and GPS decline [14], SMART Schools' −0.67 h in-school [2]. The "first stage" is not in dispute. (2) Bans reduce bullying where it has been measured with real instruments — Spain's 9.5–18% [9] and Norway's large ~0.4 SD effects [18] — and the meta-analysis finds the social-wellbeing domain is where bans have their only significant pooled effect (d = 0.22) [16]. (3) Bans do not, on current evidence, improve *average* academic achievement by much: the most precise estimates are near zero (the US national study can rule out gains above ~0.007 SD), with modest positives in specific subgroups (high-school math, lower performers) and nulls elsewhere [14]. (4) There is a consistent first-year transition cost — disciplinary incidents rose 12–15% in both Florida and the national US study before fading, and in Florida the first-year in-school suspension increase was concentrated on Black students (about 30%, with no significant effect for White or Hispanic students) [1][4]. (5) Bans do not reduce total daily phone use or improve mental wellbeing in the one study that measured both directly (SMART Schools) [2].

**Where the sources disagree — and which is stronger.** The central disagreement is the England–Sweden contrast on learning. Beland & Murphy found +0.07 SD from English bans; Kessel et al., replicating the design in Sweden with a better survey response rate and the full grade-9 population, found a precisely estimated zero and explicitly reject effects of Beland–Murphy's size [5][12]. On the merits, the Swedish null is the more robust single estimate: it uses a near-census of schools, mandatory national test data, and a ~75% response rate, whereas the English result rests on a 21%-response survey of four cities from an earlier period. But the Swedish null is also *context-bound*: Sweden is the most laptop-saturated classroom environment in Europe, so the phone was never the only screen. The fairest summary is that the English result generalised poorly, not that the English result was wrong.

A second disagreement is perception versus measurement. Australian and Dutch school-leader surveys report large perceived improvements in concentration and socialisation (75–87%) [7][10], while the US pouch study finds no improvement in *self-reported* classroom attention [14]. Neither is "wrong" — they measure different things in different informants — but a document of record should weight the pre-registered, matched-comparison, student-reported measure above principal surveys, which are vulnerable to confirmation bias from the very people who implemented the policy.

**The evidence hierarchy within this literature.** At the top are the pre-registered quasi-experiments with administrative outcomes: the US national pouch study [14] and Florida [1], plus the Indian RCT [11] for the underlying mechanism. Next are the event-study and synthetic-control designs with administrative or exam data: Norway [4], Spain [9], Sweden [12], England [5]. Below that are the cross-sectional observational comparisons (SMART Schools [2]) — informative on wellbeing and total use precisely because they measure things administrative data cannot, but unable to establish causation. At the bottom are the perception surveys (Australia, the Netherlands), which are useful for implementation and acceptability but are not evidence about outcomes. The one meta-analysis (Böttger & Zierer) is itself built on only five studies, three performance effects, and several effect sizes read off figures, and it predates all the 2025–2026 work; treat its d = 0.162 as a snapshot of the early literature, not a current estimate [16].

**Publication status matters and is easy to miss.** Much of the most-cited work is not peer-reviewed in its most-quoted form. Abrahamsson's paper circulated as an NHH discussion paper (2024) before its Journal of Human Resources version (2026) — and the published abstract's framing ("no average effect… but masks important gender differences") is more cautious than the working-paper abstract's headline. The Florida study and the US national study are NBER working papers; the Indian trial is in Science. The Spanish study is peer-reviewed but has only two treated regions. The strongest claims currently in circulation — the large Norwegian bullying effects, the Florida attendance mechanism — should be quoted with their working-paper status attached.

**What this means for policy.** The evidence supports three defensible conclusions. First, a ban reliably changes behaviour at school and is the cheapest available lever for doing so; if a jurisdiction's goal is "fewer phones in the school day," bans achieve it. Second, the downstream benefits are real but narrow and specific — reduced bullying, and modest gains for the lowest-achieving and for secondary-school mathematics — not the broad cognitive, attention and mental-health transformation often claimed. Third, the costs are front-loaded and unevenly distributed: the first-year discipline spike fell hardest on Black students in Florida, which means implementation design (what the infraction is, who is disciplined for it) is as much a policy choice as the ban itself. A jurisdiction that wants the benefits without the costs would ban the *device*, not punish the *student* — the distinction the Norwegian data support, where bullying fell regardless of strictness [18].

The single most important open fact is how little long-run evidence exists. The best studies observe at most three post-adoption years, and the policy wave that produced 58% global coverage is mostly 2023–2025. Whether the early nulls and transition costs resolve into durable gains, or whether the modest subgroup effects are the durable truth, will not be knowable until the cohort now in school sits for exams several years after their bans began.

report.title: McLuhan's Laws of Media (the Tetrad): Claims, Applications, Extensions, Critiques, and the Question of Empirical Testing
report.body:
## TL;DR

The tetrad is Marshall McLuhan's late, posthumously completed attempt to give his work a checkable form: four simultaneous questions — what a medium or artifact enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into when pushed to its limit — offered in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988) as "testable and falsifiable" scientific laws. Since 1988 scholars have applied it widely to digital objects (smartphones, games, social media, AI, online education) but almost always as a retrospective interpretive lens, and have extended it far more often than they have used it as-is — adding laws, turning it into a spiral, and privileging the reversal quadrant. The dominant critique, Tyler's "Procrustean probe," is that the tetrad is simultaneously too vague (any creative mind can fill it) and too rigid (it forces all four boxes), a charge the book's own two different wine tetrads on one page make vivid, and even its defenders concede it does not make unique, falsifiable predictions. On the empirical question, no one has tested the tetrad itself: there is no experiment, no pre-registered prediction, and no stated falsification criterion — only applications that feed evidence into the four boxes, and one diachronic counter-argument (the first media had nothing to retrieve or reverse) that remains unanswered.

## Key Findings

- The four laws, in the McLuhans' own words, ask what a medium enhances or intensifies, renders obsolete or displaces, retrieves that was previously obsolesced, and produces or becomes when pushed to an extreme; they are meant to apply simultaneously, not sequentially [11][6].
- *Laws of Media* claims scientific status: it opens by offering its observations "in testable and falsifiable form," invokes Popper, and asserts the tetrads "provide a basis for prediction" [1][8].
- The book's own authors undercut the uniqueness a law requires: Eric McLuhan said there is "not only a single correct answer" to each question [9], and the book gives two different tetrads for wine on a single page (p. 206) [3].
- Applications since 1988 cluster on digital objects — social media, smartphones, games, AI, online studios — and a systematic review of 21 Brazilian and Portuguese studies found only five reflected on the tetrad's own methodological limits [9][4][5][13].
- Extensions outnumber faithful uses: Iseri and Logan's Laws of Media Environments and Users turn the tetrad into an evolutionary spiral; Zingrone, and later Echelson/Fialka/Logan, proposed fifth laws; Levinson's "tetrad wheels" temporalize it; Logan and Mir elevate reversal [2][7][11][14].
- Tyler's critique is a double bind: too vague to be falsifiable and too rigid (Procrustean) because it forces filling all four gaps; his verdict is that calling them scientific laws is "preposterous," but they work as a heuristic probe [3].
- Even defenders concede the laws are not scientific: Logan says they "do not lead to precise results" and allow disagreement, and that McLuhan could not test them quantitatively [14][2].
- No empirical test of the tetrad itself exists: the nearest thing is Takkeci and Erdem's evidence-fed application from 20 screened empirical papers, which tests online studios, not the tetrad; and Mir's diachronic counter-example, which no one has answered with a genuine refutation [13][11].
- The only measured property of the instrument is non-reproducibility: the systematic review finds different researchers do not produce equal tetrads for the same object [9].

## Details

### 1. What the tetrad actually claims: origins, the four laws, and the book's scientific framing

The tetrad is Marshall McLuhan's late attempt to give his diffuse body of work a single, checkable form. It has a documented origin: McLuhan worked on it from 1974 until his death at the end of 1980, published it in stages in German (1974), in *Technology and Culture* (1975) and *Etc.* (1977), and it reached its finished form only in the posthumous *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988), assembled by his son Eric McLuhan. The history matters because the book's subtitle and its opening line make a specific, strong claim that the later reception largely abandoned.

The four laws are four questions asked of any medium or human artifact. The McLuhans' own formulation in the book asks what a medium enhances or intensifies, what it renders obsolete or displaces, what it retrieves that was previously obsolesced, and what it produces or becomes when pushed to an extreme [11]. The 1977 article phrased the same four as: what does it enhance; what does it obsolesce; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; what does it flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential — and added that the four features are "in analogical proportion to each other" [2]. Robert Logan, McLuhan's long-time collaborator, gives the compact form now standard in the literature: every medium or artifact (1) enhances some human function, (2) obsolesces a previous way of achieving that function, (3) retrieves something from the past that had been obsolesced earlier, and (4) when pushed to the limits of its potential, reverses or flips into an opposite or complementary form [14].

Two structural claims come with the four questions. First, simultaneity: the laws are "meant to apply simultaneously, and not linearly or sequentially" [6], and the book states explicitly that they "operate simultaneously rather than sequentially" [3]. Second, the tetrad is mapped onto McLuhan's figure/ground distinction: the enhanced medium and the new form it flips into are the two figures, while what is obsolesced and what is retrieved are the two grounds — "the LOM tetrad has two figures and two grounds" [2]. McLuhan himself, in the 1978 *English Journal* piece, described the whole approach as "a right hemisphere study which is analogical rather than logical, simultaneous rather than consecutive" [12]. Levinson's 1978 mapping, from the Tetrad Conference he organized, differs in detail (enhancement and retrieval as figures; obsolescence and reversal as grounds) [7], which is itself a small early sign of the instability that critics would later press.

The scope of the claim was always maximal. The book opens: "We found that everything man[kind] makes and does, every procedure, every style, every artefact, every poem, song, painting, gimmick, gadget, theory, technology – every product of human effort – manifested the same four dimensions" [6]. McLuhan stressed in 1975 that "only a few of them deal with communications media narrowly conceived" — the laws are about the larger ground of information and perception, and the term "media" was expanded to include inventions, ideas, philosophies and rhetorical inventions [12]. Eric McLuhan later added the key qualification that gives the game away on the scientific-status question: for each of the four questions there is not only a single correct answer, and all accurate answers are correct answers [9].

The scientific framing is what made the book controversial. The Introduction's second sentence claims the work "offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does" — hence "Laws" in the title [1]. The McLuhans said directly that Popper's statement that a scientific law is one stated so as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media [2]. The Introduction further claims the tetrads are empirical and "provide a basis for prediction, for example, that retrievals or reversals of a certain form will occur" [8], and the publisher's description called them "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [8]. McLuhan framed the laws in a Popperian spirit, inviting scholars to test their validity historically and empirically [7].

The book also issues a standing challenge that effectively defines its empirical ambition: after "more than twelve years of constant investigation," the McLuhans had found no fifth question and no single instance where one of the four laws "is clearly absent or irrelevant," and they invited readers to find either [11]. Eric McLuhan's preface records that Marshall spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law, and simultaneously for a single case in which one of the first four does not apply [11]. This is the claim — universal applicability plus falsifiability — that the entire later debate turns on, because it is simultaneously the tetrad's ambition and, as the sections below show, the point where the theory is at its weakest.

### 2. How scholars have applied the tetrad since 1988

Since 1988 the tetrad has been used far more as an interpretive lens than as a hypothesis to be confirmed, and the applications cluster around a recognizable set of objects: digital media and platforms, smartphones, games, social media, and, most recently, AI. The single most systematic picture of how the tool is actually being used in one region comes from Dall'Agnese, Canavilhas and Barichello's systematic review of applications in Brazil and Portugal between 2009 and 2019, which located 21 academic works (theses, dissertations, articles and chapters). The objects were overwhelmingly digital: "Facebook, were the most frequent theme," followed by mobile devices and interfaces, cinema, internet memes and educational platforms [9]. The review's two most important findings bear directly on the tool's status. First, the range of uses is wide and the tetrad is applied to "complex phenomena, software or hardware" [9]. Second — and this is the caveat that qualifies everything else — reflection on the tetrad as a methodological tool, or notes about its potentialities and limits based on the applications, was verified in only five of the 21 studies [9]. In other words, most of the applications are demonstrations of the framework on a chosen object, not studies of whether the framework itself works.

The canonical applications are worth stating in their full four-quadrant form, because they show both the tool's productivity and its recurring habits. On the smartphone, Adam's tetrad finds that it enhances the accessibility and convenience of the internet and accelerates real-time communication, obsolesces feature phones and reduces use of personal computers and home printers, retrieves earlier obsolesced functions, and — in the reversal quadrant — flips, when pushed to its extreme, toward augmented-reality devices such as Google Glass that might render users oblivious to their surroundings and restrict rather than facilitate interaction [4]. On digital games, Tyler's own application (made while arguing the tool is not science) finds that games enhance diverse modes of play, obsolesce traditional television viewing, retrieve lost means of participation, and reverse into pervasive and persistent play [3]. On social media, Logan's tetrad enhances online connections and non-local friendships, obsolesces face-to-face socialization and real life, retrieves long-distance correspondence together with what he calls Narcissus and masquerade, and reverses into social isolation, virtual life, fake identities and fake news [14]. On AI and large language models in education, López finds the technologies "enhance personalized learning, obsolesce traditional assessment practices, retrieve transmission-model pedagogies, and risk reversing into environments of cognitive offloading, epistemic dependency, and automated academic fraud" [5].

The most methodologically self-conscious recent application is Takkeci and Erdem's 2024 study of online architectural design-studio education, which is notable because it tries to keep the hermeneutic claims tethered to evidence. They state plainly that "the functionality of the tetrad is not based on theoretical grounds, but revolves around four questions based on empirical observation" [13], and they built the application on a two-stage systematic review: an initial set of nine papers was expanded by snowballing to 176 records of peer-reviewed empirical studies, screened down to 20 papers read in full, whose findings were then extracted, thematized and organized into the four quadrants [13]. Their conclusions for online studio education — that it enhances accessibility and participation across distances, obsolesces aspects of the physical studio's tacit, tactile pedagogy, retrieves overlooked design history and theory, and reverses the instructor-student hierarchy toward more student-led and democratic, or alternately depersonalized and transactional, forms [13] — are a good illustration of the strongest form the tetrad can take in practice: each quadrant is a synthesis of empirical findings rather than a free association.

Two patterns run across all of these applications and are important for assessing the tetrad honestly. First, the same object routinely generates different, non-identical tetrads, and the tradition treats this as a feature: Gouzouasis and LaMonde, in an early arts-based-education application, state that individual tetrads are neither exclusive nor definitive, and they read the book's own multiple tetrads for the same medium as deliberate [10]. Second, the applications are almost always retrospective diagnosis. The smartphone, games, social media and online-studio tetrads are all built from effects already observed in the literature, then slotted into four boxes. That is why, as the next two sections show, the tetrad has been so durable as a pedagogical and interpretive device and so weak as a predictive or empirical instrument.

### 3. How scholars have extended or reformulated the tetrad

The extensions fall into three families: those that generalize the tetrad's internal logic, those that add new laws, and those that press the fourth law specifically.

The most consequential formal extension is Iseri and Logan's, which holds that when an artifact is pushed far enough, it is not only the artifact that flips: its environment and its users flip too. They extend the original Laws of Media (LOM) into two parallel sets — Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU) [2]. Their reading makes the tetrad an evolutionary model, explaining the continuous emergence of new artifacts in the ongoing cycle of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and flip, with each cycle linked to the previous and the next in a spiral [2]. The same authors explicitly acknowledge that this is where the framework leaves the territory of scientific law, since the LOM "does not make unique predictions" about what will be retrieved or what a medium will flip into, and there is "often more than one correct answer" to the four questions [2]. On this extension, the tetrad is a spiral of artifact evolution, and the "flip" of one cycle seeds the enhancement quadrant of the next — a diachronic reading of a tool the McLuhans insisted was synchronic.

The fifth-law literature is smaller but revealing. *Laws of Media* explicitly challenged readers to find a fifth question applying to all media or a single counter-instance where one of the four fails [11]. Frank Zingrone's 1991 answer, the best-known attempt, was a law of syncretism — the fusion of technologies into hybrids — which Lindia and Levinson note collapses back into enhancement, retrieval, or both, and so was not accepted [7]. Echelson, Fialka and Logan (2022) proposed a counterfactual fifth question: "What would have happened—or not happened—if a tool, medium, or artifact had not been invented or developed?" — applied, for example, to the question of whether zero would have emerged without the alphabet and abacus [11]. Graham Harman's response to the whole enterprise is the most principled: the tetrad necessarily cannot extend beyond its four poles, because the four poles embody the four possible figure/ground relationships [7]. On Harman's reading the fourfold is closed by construction, which is exactly why a fifth law keeps failing.

Levinson's "tetrad wheels," first proposed at the 1978 Tetrad Conference he organized at Fairleigh Dickinson University and only formally published by Lindia and Levinson in 2021, are the main attempt to make the tetrad move through time. Their stated purpose is to extend McLuhan's original tetrads by exploring how the figure/ground structures move the tetrads from synchronic analysis to diachronic analysis [7]. This matters because the McLuhans had described the four laws as simultaneous, a snapshot rather than a sequence; the tetrad wheel chains those snapshots so that the reversal of one medium becomes the retrieval or enhancement of the next.

The most active contemporary line concerns the fourth law, reversal. Logan's 2021 *McLuhan in Reverse* argues that thinking in reversals was McLuhan's master pattern, that "the medium is the message" is itself a reversal, and — the substantive claim most relevant to the present — that digital media flipped McLuhan's "media as extensions of man" into its opposite: a reversal has taken place in which the users of digital media have become extensions of their media, as the data they enter becomes part of the system they are interacting with [14]. Andrey Mir has pushed the reversal quadrant furthest, in two directions that are really criticisms of the framework's integrity. His diachronic objection is that the tetrad is a synchronic grammar that breaks when read historically: "At the beginning of time (of media evolution), the first media had nothing to retrieve, as there were no prior media effects. At the beginning of time, the first media also had nothing to reverse, as they had not yet reached their extremes or limits" [11]. So the first human media could only enhance and obsolesce, and Mir's inference is that the four laws apply fully only in the slow middle stretch of media history, not at its origin or, under digital acceleration, at its end. Carlos Scolari has replied from within the tradition that detaching reversal from the other three laws is dangerous: taking the Law of Reversal to its extreme results in an out-of-control interpretive explosion, at which point the other three laws cease to function as balancing rods [11]. The exchange between Mir and Scolari is, in effect, an argument about whether the tetrad is one balanced instrument or four separable claims — and it shows that the strongest recent extension (treating reversal as the dominant law of the digital age) is also the sharpest recent challenge to the tetrad's simultaneity.

One structural point unites all of these extensions. Whether the move is to generalize (Iseri and Logan), to add (Zingrone; Echelson, Fialka and Logan), to temporalize (Levinson's wheels), or to privilege one law (Logan, Mir), every extension treats the original fourfold as incomplete or in need of rebalancing. That is a fact about the reception worth stating plainly: the tetrad has been extended far more often than it has been used as-is, and the direction of every extension has been away from the book's claim that the four questions are universal, simultaneous, and sufficient.

### 4. The critiques: Tyler's Procrustean argument and the falsifiability debate

The sharpest and best-documented critique is Tom Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe" (*Game Studies*, 2008), and it is worth reconstructing in full because it is a double objection, not the single "too vague" objection it is often reduced to. Tyler's opening states the thesis: considered as a scientific theory, the tetrad risks violating communications research "in a dangerously Procrustean manner," but conceived as an exploratory probe it can be illuminating. His named fear is that the tetrad operates like the bandit Procrustes, forcing "bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory" to be hammered or shorn so that they fit. His first objection is looseness: the tetrad is far too vague, because a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse into, so the laws do not lend themselves to falsification because examples can readily be stretched to fit. His second objection is the opposite: just like Procrustes' bed, the tetrad is unrelentingly rigid, because it requires the analyst to fill all four gaps whether or not the evidence supports four answers [3].

The evidence Tyler offers is internal to the book. On a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206), the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine: one in which wine enhances grape juice, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance and reverses into cooking wine vinegar; and an alternative on the same page in which it enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [3]. Tyler's inference is that if the authors cannot agree with themselves on one page, "it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" — a direct rebuttal of the book's claim that the answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time. His verdict on the scientific claim is blunt: the idea that these are scientific laws in the ordinary sense of the phrase is preposterous [3]. Yet he does not abandon the tool: the diversity of results is acceptable once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity, so long as the applications are illuminating, and he concludes the tetrad is best used as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions [3].

Tyler's critique was not the first, and its roots go back to the book's own reception. McLuhan had invited falsification in 1975, and the first sustained response, William Henry Venable's "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (*Technology and Culture*, 1976), read the laws through C. S. Peirce's logic of signs. McLuhan's published reply conceded the point while denying the contact: the tetrads are analogical, with no connections between any of them but dynamic ratios, and between his position and Venable's there was simply no point of contact whatever [12]. In other words, the first time a critic took the testability claim seriously, McLuhan retreated from logic to analogy — a move that later commentators read as the theory giving up its own Popperian pretension. Contemporary critics repeat the same diagnosis in Popperian terms: Basbaum argues the tetrad's testability is doubtful "in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim" [1].

Even the tetrad's own advocates concede the core of this. Logan, who has done more than anyone to extend the tetrad, writes that the Laws of Media "are not strictly scientific laws," because they do not make unique predictions about what will be retrieved or what a medium will flip into, and there is "often more than one correct answer" to the four questions [2]. He elsewhere distinguishes the three senses of law explicitly: scientific laws make precise, falsifiable predictions; legal laws are changeable by legislatures; and McLuhan's laws are probes and hypotheses that do not lead to precise results, because different users of the tool can legitimately disagree [14]. And a reviewer of the book on its own terms noted the practical gap: the book contains "no experiments proposed as to how a tetrad may be tested, no indication of what the criteria for a successful falsification might be, and no general or specific methods for properly determining predictive power" [8].

The empirical literature, thin as it is, supplies the clearest independent confirmation of the non-uniqueness objection. Dall'Agnese, Canavilhas and Barichello's systematic review concludes: "even if analyses of the four processes (enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal) are constructed based on the same empirical objects, we will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads" [9]. The book itself provides multiple tetrads for the same medium on pp. 196–207, which some defenders read as deliberate — Gouzouasis and LaMonde describe individual tetrads as "neither exclusive nor definitive" [10]. But the two readings of the same fact are in tension: what the tradition defends as richness is, from the Popperian standpoint McLuhan himself invoked, the absence of a unique observable consequence.

The defensible synthesis, visible across both critics and advocates, is that the tetrad is a generative probe whose outputs are hypotheses, not findings. Tyler's constructive conditions are the best statement of what a disciplined use looks like: anchor each quadrant in cited research, define the quadrant terms (obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction; reversal as an already-present potential rather than a forecast), report where evidence cuts against a quadrant, narrow the scope on purpose, and aim each quadrant at a specific misconception rather than filling four boxes [3]. Under those conditions the tetrad earns its keep as a question-asking instrument. What it cannot earn, on its own evidence, is the status its subtitle claims — a "new science" whose laws are testable and falsifiable in the Popperian sense the McLuhans themselves invoked.

### 5. Has anyone tested the tetrad empirically?

The short, honest answer is no: no one has tested the tetrad as a set of laws in the way McLuhan claimed they could be tested. There is no published experimental or quantitative study that operationalizes the four laws, states a falsifiable prediction derived from them, and reports a pass or fail. The reasons for this absence are themselves documented in the literature, and they matter as much as the absence.

McLuhan did invite the test, and the invitation is on the record. His 1975 and 1977 articles appealed to scholars to test the laws' validity historically and empirically [7], and the book restated the challenge as finding a fifth question or a counter-instance where one of the four laws fails [11]. But the invitation went effectively unanswered in the form in which it was issued. Logan, the tradition's most active exponent, states the situation from the inside: unlike the natural sciences, McLuhan could not test his hypotheses quantitatively, so he had to be content with his probes [14]. That is an admission by a defender that the framework was never put through anything like a quantitative test, and that its own originator treated it as a probe rather than a verified regularity.

What exists instead of tests are two weaker things, and it is important not to conflate either of them with empirical confirmation of the laws.

The first is application-to-evidence: studies that feed real data into the four boxes but never test whether the four boxes themselves hold. The clearest recent example is Takkeci and Erdem's 2024 study of online design-studio education, which is as close as the literature comes to an empirical tetrad. It grounded each quadrant in a systematic review of 20 empirical papers out of 176 candidate records, and it produced a specific, evidence-carrying tetrad (enhances accessibility; obsolesces aspects of the tactile, physical studio; retrieves design history and theory; reverses toward either democratized or depersonalized learning) [13]. But the study tests the effects of online studios, not the tetrad: the tetrad is the organizing device, and there is no control, no prediction registered in advance, and no way for the framework to fail. The same is true of the Brazilian and Portuguese applications the systematic review catalogues, which use the tetrad to organize observations about Facebook, mobile interfaces, cinema, memes and educational platforms [9]. Feeding evidence into a framework is not the same as testing the framework.

The second is the unfilled negative challenge. The closest thing to a falsification attempt in the entire literature is not empirical but conceptual: Andrey Mir's diachronic counter-example. Mir argues that the first human media — fire, clothing, the digging stick — could not have retrieved anything, because there were no prior media effects to retrieve, and could not have reversed, because they had not been pushed to their extremes; so at the origin of media history only enhancement and obsolescence apply [11]. This is a genuine attempt to produce the counter-instance the McLuhans said did not exist, and to that extent it is the one place where the tetrad's universality claim has been put to a test of the kind the book demanded. But it is a thought experiment about prehistory, not an empirical observation, and defenders can (and do) reply that fire "retrieves" the sun or that the digging stick retrieves claws and tusks — which is precisely the looseness Tyler identified: the categories are elastic enough to absorb almost any counter-example.

Two further facts complete the picture. First, the one empirical regularity the literature has actually documented about the tetrad is its non-reproducibility: the systematic review finds that even for the same empirical object, different researchers will not produce equal tetrads [9]. If one takes "testable and falsifiable" seriously, that is a measured property of the instrument — low inter-analyst agreement — and it is the opposite of what a scientific law requires. Second, the book's own failure to specify test conditions was noted immediately on publication: a reviewer observed that it proposed no experiments, no criteria for a successful falsification, and no method for determining predictive power [8]. A theory cannot be empirically tested, let alone confirmed, if its own text never states what would count as a disconfirming observation; and the strongest case that the tetrad could not be falsified is that, in four decades, nobody has been able to state one either.

What this does not mean should also be said plainly. The absence of an empirical test of the laws is not evidence that individual tetrad applications are wrong or useless; the applications in section 2 show they can organize findings and surface overlooked effects. It means that the tetrad's empirical status is exactly what its critics and its defenders, unusually, agree on: it is a heuristic or probe that generates interpretive hypotheses, not a scientific law that has been — or perhaps can be — empirically confirmed.


## Beyond this question

For anyone working with the tetrad, the practical lesson is already settled on both sides of the debate: use it as a generator of rival hypotheses, not as a finding. Tyler's conditions — anchor each quadrant in cited evidence, define the quadrant terms, report contrary evidence, narrow scope, and aim each quadrant at a named misconception — are a ready-made quality bar, and the two-wine example is the clearest demonstration of why a single tetrad should never be published as if it were the tetrad. The systematic-review finding that different analysts produce non-identical tetrads for the same object is the single most useful empirical fact about the tool, and it counsels the same thing: treat disagreement between two tetrads as data, not noise.

There is also a concrete, unoccupied opportunity here. The literature contains many applications and many critiques but no study that measures the instrument itself — for example, whether independent analysts converge on the same quadrants for the same artifact, whether a tetrad stated before a technology matures predicts its later reversal, or whether tetrad prompts outperform plain questions at surfacing overlooked effects. The one respect in which the tetrad genuinely resembles a scientific instrument is that its performance characteristics could be measured; no one has done it.

## Open questions

The central open question is the one the McLuhans themselves posed and no one has answered under controlled conditions: can a falsifiable prediction be derived from the four laws that fails when the facts come in? Four decades after publication, there is no published experiment, no quantitative test, and no stated falsification criterion anywhere in the secondary literature, and the book itself states none. Until someone specifies in advance what observation would refute a tetrad, the claim that the laws are testable remains an unfilled promissory note.

Several narrower questions follow from the record:

- **Inter-analyst reliability has never been measured.** The systematic review documents that different researchers produce different tetrads for the same object, but no study has quantified how much divergence there is, or whether trained analysts converge more than untrained ones.
- **No prediction has been registered in advance.** The reversal quadrant in particular is only ever applied retrospectively; there is no ledger of forward-looking reversal predictions with a resolution rate, which is the minimum needed to test the book's claim that the laws allow prediction.
- **The counter-example question is unresolved.** Mir's diachronic argument (first media had nothing to retrieve or reverse) is the only serious attempt at the counter-instance the book demanded, and it has not been answered in print except by the kind of elastic re-description (fire "retrieves" the sun) that Tyler identified as the theory's looseness.
- **Coverage was thin in two places.** I could not read the full Venable (1976) exchange — the primary letters are paywalled and McLuhan's reply is known through excerpts and the McLuhan Studies archive — and the 1978 Tetrad Conference proceedings remain formally unpublished, known through Lindia and Levinson's 2021 reclamation. Both would sharpen the historical record of the first falsification debate.
- **The strongest untested claim is Harman's.** Harman's argument that the four poles exhaust the figure/ground possibilities would, if worked out formally, show whether the tetrad is a closed taxonomy (always applicable by construction) or an open empirical claim — and that distinction is exactly what separates a probe from a law.

The honest bottom line on the empirical question is that "has anyone tested it" has a yes-and-no structure. Yes: scholars have repeatedly fed empirical evidence into the tetrad, and one study (Takkeci and Erdem) did so systematically from a screened corpus of 20 empirical papers. No: no one has tested the tetrad itself — its universality, its simultaneity, or its predictive power — against a stated possibility of failure.
